entities.name: All Nations Pentecostal Church
entities.description: Bronzeville Pentecostal congregation founded by a formerly enslaved-generation Georgia migrant woman; healing ministry, interracial membership, radio pioneer, Depression-era feeding program.

claims.claim: Elder Lucy Smith (born Lucinda Madden, Woodstock, Georgia) arrived in Chicago in 1910, began home prayer meetings in 1916, and established the Langley Avenue All Nations Pentecostal Church in 1920; the purpose-built church was completed December 1926.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Birth year given as 1874 in the encyclopedia entry vs. 1875 in devotional accounts (e.g., TikTok post); minor discrepancy, does not affect institutional dates.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Elder Lucy Smith': arrived Chicago 1910 after joining Pentecostal Stone Church by 1912; home prayer meetings 1916; church established 1920; building completed Dec. 1926 -- described as 'the first church in Chicago ever established by a woman pastor.' Wallace Best (2007), via review: documents Smith's ministry as founder of All Nations Pentecostal Church and her interracial Bronzeville congregation.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Elder Lucy Smith'; Free Library review of Best (2007)
claims.uncertainty: Biographical dates rest on a tertiary source (Wikipedia); Best's book is the scholarly anchor but the review summary does not independently confirm each date. Treat founding dates as Provisional pending archival confirmation.

claims.claim: All Nations ran a Depression-era feeding ministry ('feeding thousands'), a gospel music ministry, and was one of the first African American churches to broadcast worship services on radio.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Elder Lucy Smith': 'developed an active community outreach program, feeding thousands during the Great Depression... All Nations was one of the first African American churches to broadcast worship services on the radio.' Best (2007) review: Best uses radio broadcasting as a lens on migrant/urban religious culture interplay; centers Smith's vibrant Pentecostal worship and interracial congregation.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Elder Lucy Smith'; Best (2007) via review
claims.uncertainty: 'Feeding thousands' and 'first to broadcast' are unquantified superlatives from the tertiary source; Best confirms the radio and community-activity themes in substance.

entities.name: Apostolic Church of God
entities.description: Woodlawn megachurch (20,000+ members per its development materials), a spiritual anchor in Woodlawn since the 1930s. Led for 48 years by Bishop Arthur M. Brazier; now led by Dr. J. Byron Brazier. Self-developing the Woodlawn Central district through ACOG Ventures LLC.

claims.claim: The Apostolic Church of God has served as a spiritual anchor in Woodlawn since the 1930s and, under Bishop Arthur M. Brazier and now Dr. Byron Brazier, created the vision and plan for Woodlawn Central, establishing the Network of Woodlawn in 2015 and the 2060 Woodlawn Community Plan.
claims.evidence: viv-media.com / Woodlawn Central materials: 'The Apostolic Church of God, which has served as a spiritual anchor in Woodlawn since the 1930s, created the vision and plan for Woodlawn Central with recommendations from The Network of Woodlawn, a community-building collaborative ACOG helped establish in 2015.' J. Byron Brazier op-ed, Black Enterprise, Sept 28, 2026.
claims.source: woodlawncentral.com; J. Byron Brazier, 'Development Without Displacement Is a Capital Strategy, Not a Slogan,' Black Enterprise, September 28, 2026
claims.uncertainty: Membership figure (20,000+) and 1930s anchor claim come from the church's own development materials.

claims.claim: Bishop Arthur M. Brazier, as president of The Woodlawn Organization in the 1960s, worked with Saul Alinsky to limit the University of Chicago's expansion into Woodlawn, modeling church-led land control as community power.
claims.evidence: J. Byron Brazier op-ed (Black Enterprise, 2026): 'In the 1960s, as president of The Woodlawn Organization, he worked alongside Saul Alinsky to limit the University of Chicago's expansion into our neighborhood.'
claims.source: J. Byron Brazier, Black Enterprise, September 28, 2026
claims.uncertainty: Family memoir framing; TWO's Alinsky collaboration is independently well documented (see TWO entity).

entities.name: Bethel AME Church
entities.description: African Methodist Episcopal congregation at 4440 S. Michigan Ave., Chicago (Grand Boulevard/Bronzeville). Organized 1862 as a mission church of Quinn Chapel by Bishop William Paul Quinn; occupied 17 locations before settling at its current site in 1949; celebrated its 155th anniversary in 2017.

claims.claim: First organized in June 1862 as a mission church by Bishop William Paul Quinn, due to overcrowding at Quinn Chapel AME Church.
claims.evidence: The Christian Recorder (the AME Church's official newspaper) 155th-anniversary article states this origin directly.
claims.source: The Christian Recorder, 'Bethel AME Church, Chicago, Celebrates 155 Years' (c. 2017).
claims.uncertainty: Denominational-newspaper account consistent with Quinn Chapel's growth history; the exact June 1862 organization is single-sourced to anniversary coverage.

claims.claim: Bethel occupied 17 different locations from its 1862 inception until 1949, when it moved to its current location at 4440 S. Michigan Ave.
claims.evidence: The Christian Recorder anniversary article.
claims.source: The Christian Recorder (c. 2017).
claims.uncertainty: Single source; the 17-location figure and 1949 move date are the congregation's anniversary claims.

claims.claim: Celebrated its 155th anniversary on the weekend of June 24-25, 2017, under the pastorate of Rev. Jennifer Tinsley, with Bishop Anne Henning Byfield as anniversary preacher.
claims.evidence: The Christian Recorder article documenting the event.
claims.source: The Christian Recorder (c. 2017).
claims.uncertainty: None on the event itself; living clergy named only in their public roles.

entities.name: Bishop Archibald J. Carey Sr.
entities.description: AME bishop; pastor of Quinn Chapel AME from 1898; father of Archibald Carey Jr.; an early example of Black Chicago clergy holding municipal appointments through Republican machine ties.

claims.claim: Carey Sr. became pastor of Quinn Chapel AME Church in 1898.
claims.evidence: In 1898, Archibald Carey Sr. became pastor of Quinn Chapel.
claims.source: The TRiiBE, 'The rise of Black political power in early Chicago' (quoting Chicago History Museum senior VP John Russick)
claims.uncertainty: Low. Corroborated by Dennis C. Dickerson's peer-reviewed book African American Preachers and Politics: The Careys of Chicago.

claims.claim: Carey Sr. campaigned for the Republican Party, allied with Mayor William Hale Thompson, and was appointed Chicago's chief examiner of claims and a civil service commissioner, using the posts to advance Black hiring and discipline abusive officers.
claims.evidence: He campaigned for the Republican party and got close with William Thompson, who would eventually become Chicago's mayor in 1915. Through his relationships, Carey later became the city's chief examiner of claims and a civil service commissioner, where he made sure the city hired more Black police and punished officers who unfairly treated Black people.
claims.source: The TRiiBE, 'The rise of Black political power in early Chicago'
claims.uncertainty: Moderate on exact dates of each appointment; the offices themselves are corroborated by Dickerson's book ('When the mayor appointed Carey to the city's civil service commission, Carey helped in the hiring and promotion of local blacks').

claims.claim: Carey Sr.'s tenure on the civil service commission was marred by allegations of impropriety involving the sale of jobs.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located; resolution of the allegations is Unresolved.
claims.evidence: But alleged impropriety for selling jobs marred the bishop's tenure.
claims.source: Dennis C. Dickerson, African American Preachers and Politics: The Careys of Chicago (book description/summary)
claims.uncertainty: The claim appears in the book's summary; the underlying primary record (charges, proceedings) was not located in this research pass. Treat as allegation, not established fact.

entities.name: Bishop Arthur M. Brazier
entities.description: Pastor of the Apostolic Church of God, Woodlawn, 1960-2008; diocesan bishop, Pentecostal Assemblies of the World; founder/spokesman of The Woodlawn Organization; co-founder of the Coordinating Council of Community Organizations; community-development leader.

claims.claim: Brazier was pastor of the Apostolic Church of God in Chicago's Woodlawn neighborhood from 1960 to 2008 and diocesan bishop of the 6th Episcopal District of the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World.
claims.evidence: served as diocesan bishop of the 6th Episcopal District of the Pentecostal Assemblies of the World, in addition to his work as pastor of the Chicago's Apostolic Church of God. (HistoryMakers); In office 1960-2008 (pastor). (Wikipedia infobox)
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A2005_003); Wikipedia
claims.uncertainty: Low.
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit 2026-09-28: source_type primary -> secondary. Source mixes an institutional/finding-aid reference with Wikipedia or weak components; "primary" is reserved for primary records directly consulted and establishing the fact. Source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A2005_003); Wikipedia

claims.claim: Brazier was a founder and spokesman of the (Temporary) Woodlawn Organization (TWO) around 1960-61, organized with Saul Alinsky's Industrial Areas Foundation, and led TWO's fight against University of Chicago expansion in 1963.
claims.evidence: Brazier became the spokesman for the Temporary Woodlawn Organization (TWO), organized by Nicholas Von Hoffman of Saul Alinsky's Industrial Areas Foundation. Brazier successfully led TWO against the expansion of the University of Chicago in 1963. (HistoryMakers); In 1960, this local church leader was one of the founders of and became the spokesman for The Woodlawn Organization (TWO) (Nonprofit Quarterly, 2010)
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A2005_003); Nonprofit Quarterly (citing the Chicago Defender, 2010-03-24)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Brazier co-founded the Coordinating Council of Community Organizations (CCCO) with Bill Berry of the Chicago Urban League to fight school segregation; he resigned in 1965 but worked with Al Raby during Dr. King's 1966 Chicago visit.
claims.evidence: With Bill Berry of the Chicago Urban League, Brazier also formed the Coordinating Council of Community Organizations which fought segregation in Chicago's public schools; he resigned in 1965, but was active with Al Raby in Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s visit to Chicago in 1966. (HistoryMakers)
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A2005_003)
claims.uncertainty: Low on founding and resignation; the precise circumstances of the 1965 resignation are not detailed in the finding aid.

claims.claim: In later decades Brazier chaired the Woodlawn Children's Promise Community and was named the first Senior Fellow of the Local Initiatives Support Corporation (LISC) Chicago program.
claims.evidence: Most recently Brazier served as chair of the Woodlawn Children's Promise Community... At a 2008 event to honor Brazier's selection as the first Senior Fellow of the Local Initiatives Support Corporation
claims.source: University of Chicago News obituary, 2010
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Black Spiritualist Storefront Churches
entities.description: Black Spiritualist storefront tradition in Chicago: healing-and-prophecy-oriented small churches, part of the storefront phenomenon from the 1930s onward.

claims.claim: Black Spiritual/Spiritualist churches were one of the three denominational concentrations of Chicago's storefront churches in 1930 and persisted as named storefronts into the 1960s (e.g., Traveling Souls Spiritual Church, Healing Water Spiritual Church, St. Mary's Faith Spiritual Church, The Vineyard Spiritual Temple).
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; Spiritualist presence is smaller than Baptist but consistently documented.
claims.evidence: Mays & Nicholson (1933) via Boyd (1998): storefronts concentrated in Baptist, Holiness, Spiritualist. Noreen (1965): 16 of 381 names (4%) designated Pentecostal or Spiritualist. Stronks (1964): lists multiple Spiritual churches/temples on West Roosevelt Road.
claims.source: Mays & Nicholson (1933) via Boyd (1998); Noreen (1965); Stronks (1964)
claims.uncertainty: Scholarship on Black Spiritual churches specifically (as distinct from Spiritualism generally) is thin; their internal history in Chicago is not documented in the sources found.

entities.name: Chicago Conference on Religion and Race
entities.description: Interfaith coalition that coordinated the 'summit' negotiations between the Chicago Freedom Movement, Mayor Richard J. Daley, business leaders, and real estate officials in August 1966.

claims.claim: The Chicago Conference on Religion and Race coordinated the August 17, 1966 summit meeting that produced the Summit Agreement on open housing.
claims.evidence: Indiana Law Review, Vol. 41: 'The Chicago Conference on Religion and Race coordinated the so-called "summit" meeting, which convened on August 17, 1966. Participants included the Mayor, his colleagues and advisors, CFM leaders, business leaders, and leaders of the Chicago Real Estate Board.'
claims.source: Indiana Law Review, Vol. 41, 'Non-Violent Direct Action and the Legislative Process' (mckinneylaw.iu.edu)
claims.uncertainty: Law-review account with citations to Garrow and others; primary summit records not consulted.

entities.name: Church Mothers
entities.description: The senior women's leadership office in Black Baptist, Methodist, and Sanctified congregations: a recognized moral authority operating alongside (and checking) pastoral authority.

claims.claim: The Church Mother is an older woman of exemplary Christian standing, publicly addressed as 'Mother,' whose seat is formally or informally reserved (and may be draped in black at her death), who consults with the pastor on daily issues of discipline and doctrine, and who accumulates prestige and real authority over long service.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; role varies by congregation and denomination (Baptist, Methodist, Sanctified/Pentecostal/Holiness/Apostolic).
claims.evidence: Cheryl Townsend Gilkes, 'The Politics of "Silence"' (1997), p. 92, quoted in a Vanderbilt dissertation chapter: Church Mother as the distinctive feature of 'dual-sex church politics,' foil/counter to the pastor, with members soliciting her advice, permission, and prayers.
claims.source: Cheryl Townsend Gilkes (1997), in African American Christianity: Essays in History (ed. Paul E. Johnson)
claims.uncertainty: Documented for Black churches generally (Baptist, Methodist, Sanctified traditions); Chicago-specific small-congregation instances are not individually documented in the sources found.

entities.name: Church of God in Christ (Chicago presence)
entities.description: The Pentecostal denomination rooted in the Holiness movement whose Chicago congregations formed a significant share of the storefront landscape.

claims.claim: COGIC spread to Chicago with the Great Migration from its Holiness-movement roots (founded 1897 by Bishop Charles Harrison Mason); its congregations appear in Chicago's storefront landscape (30 of 381 names, 8%, in Noreen's 1965 survey).
claims.evidence: History-of-COGIC summary (itslibres.edu.mx PDF): founded 1897 by Bishop Charles Harrison Mason in Little Rock, Arkansas; Great Migration contributed to COGIC's spread including Chicago. Noreen (1965): 30 churches designated 'Church of God in Christ' among 381 storefront names. Spear (1967): post-migration growth of small Holiness and Pentecostal groups in Chicago.
claims.source: Noreen (1965); Spear (1967); COGIC history summary
claims.uncertainty: The 1897 founding account comes from a low-authority web PDF; treat founding details as Provisional. Noreen's 8% figure is observational data.

entities.name: Church Program & Choir Anniversary Economy
entities.description: The Black church program economy: choir anniversaries, musicals, and sheet-music sales through church networks that funded and circulated gospel music.

claims.claim: The first gospel choir appeared in the 1930s at Pilgrim Baptist Church in Chicago; choir anniversaries/'Choir Day' became a central Black church institution acknowledging music ministry, and church musical programs and anniversaries sustained the gospel economy.
claims.evidence: Tammy L. Kernodle (musicologist, Miami University), African American Lectionary: 'Since the first gospel choir appeared in the 1930s at the Pilgrim Baptist Church in Chicago, it has remained one of the most recognized symbols of Black Church culture... the one unifying agent... is the celebration of Choir Day or the Choir Anniversary. This celebration, outside of the annual concerts or musical programs, is one of the few moments within the life of the Black Church in which the importance of the ministry of music... is acknowledged.'
claims.source: The African American Lectionary, 'Choir Anniversary' cultural resources (Kernodle)
claims.uncertainty: Scholarly essay, not an economic study; quantifies the cultural role rather than dollar flows of the church-program economy. Red-team harmonization (2026-09-28): primacy disputed between Pilgrim and Ebenezer (both 1931 claims); Dorsey employment timeline needed.

claims.claim: Dorsey's sheet-music sales model depended on church networks: Frye and Sallie Martin were 'two of the first and most effective singers Dorsey took with him to market his work,' rehearsing sales pitches and traveling to churches in and around Chicago.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (Dorsey), citing scholarship: Dorsey 'worked with numerous musicians who assisted in selling his sheet music traveling to churches in and around Chicago. Rehearsals for sales pitches took place in Dorsey's nearly bare room in his uncle's house. Frye and Sallie Martin were two of the first and most effective singers Dorsey took with him to market his work.'
claims.source: Wikipedia (Thomas A. Dorsey)
claims.uncertainty: Drawn from secondary gospel-music scholarship (Heilbut); Defender-era documentation of church-program commerce not retrieved.

claims.claim: James Cleveland sang as a boy soprano at Pilgrim Baptist under Dorsey with Roberta Martin as choir pianist, later founded the Gospel Music Workshop of America (1967/1968) — the institutional successor to the NCGCC model.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Many references date GMWA's founding convention to 1967; sources found here say 1968.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'Born in Chicago, Cleveland began singing as a boy soprano at Pilgrim Baptist Church where Thomas A. Dorsey was minister of music and Roberta Martin was pianist for the choir.' Archive liner notes: 'He began The Gospel Music Workshop of America in 1968.' Exampleessays also dates the GMWA's founding convention to 1968.
claims.source: Wikipedia (James Cleveland); Internet Archive album liner notes; exampleessays.com
claims.uncertainty: GMWA founding year is commonly given as 1967 or 1968; these sources say 1968. Cleveland is included as a church-side figure rather than a separate entity because his full biography belongs to the industry track.

entities.name: Congregational Mutual Aid
entities.description: The sickness-relief, burial, and newcomer-support functions of small congregations: pooled pennies for burial, aid in illness, and migrant reception networks.

claims.claim: Congregants pooled small sums 'in order to aid each other in time of sickness but more especially to insure themselves a decent Christian burial,' forming the base of church-rooted mutual-aid and burial societies that grew into Black-owned insurance enterprises.
claims.contradictory_evidence: William Montgomery (cited in Harris) cautions that by the turn of the century Black churches 'did not always rank as the most important community service agencies' because members were poor and mortgage debt constrained charity -- i.e., the mutual-aid capacity was real but limited.
claims.evidence: E. Franklin Frazier (quoted in Harris, 'Black Churches and Civic Traditions'): church-rooted mutual-aid societies were 'inspired by the spirit of Christian charity' where congregants 'scrapped together pennies.' Lincoln & Mamiya (1990), via HUD compendium: 'Congregations became seedbeds for organizing mutual aid societies, banks, businesses, schools, and medical facilities.' Boyd (1998), citing Butler (1991): 'The fundamental institution for self-help among Afro-Americans was the church.'
claims.publication_date: Frazier (1964 ed.); Lincoln & Mamiya (1990); Harris (chapter, n.d.)
claims.source: Frazier via Harris; Lincoln & Mamiya (1990); Butler (1991) via Boyd (1998)
claims.uncertainty: These are general Black-church findings; no source found documents a specific Chicago storefront congregation's sickness or burial fund by name. Montgomery's caution about financial constraints applies especially to small congregations.

claims.claim: Migrant congregations reproduced home-community care networks: new arrivals organized churches with former townsmen; women's auxiliaries ran meal programs and clothing drives; churches were the first stop for housing, employment information, childcare, and emergency financial support.
claims.evidence: Boyd (1998) citing Grossman (1989): migrants organized churches 'frequently joining with former townsmen or other dissatisfied migrants seeking an alternative'; a Chicago migrant quoted in Grossman left a large church because 'it don't see the small people....The preacher wouldn't know me...at home whenever I didn't come to Sunday School they would always come and see what was the matter.' Nonprofit Quarterly (2026): 'In Chicago, Detroit, and Harlem, Black churches frequently became the first stop for new arrivals... Women's auxiliaries organized meal programs and clothing drives.'
claims.source: James Grossman, Land of Hope (1989), via Boyd (1998); Nonprofit Quarterly (2026)
claims.uncertainty: The Grossman material covers migrants generally; the Nonprofit Quarterly piece is recent journalism synthesizing scholarship rather than a primary study.

entities.name: Contemporary Storefront Churches (South/West Sides)
entities.description: The living continuation of the storefront tradition on the South and West sides: small, idiosyncratic, neighborhood-embedded congregations documented photographically and journalistically in the 21st century.

claims.claim: Small African American community churches in repurposed commercial spaces continued operating on Chicago's South and West sides into the 2000s-2020s, with individualized identities, hand-lettered signage, and neighborhood-embedded membership.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; scale relative to the mid-20th century is not quantified in any source found.
claims.evidence: Dave Jordano, Articles of Faith (2009): five years photographing South/West side storefront churches; congregants create 'a comforting environment of affirmation, hope, and family.' WBEZ Curious City (Jan. 25, 2024): storefront churches 'have been around since the early 1900s' and remain in operation in South and West side neighborhoods like Austin. Rogers Park/West Ridge Historical Society: 'Some congregations eventually grow beyond the storefront... some remain in place for many years, providing sacred space for a close family of worshipers.'
claims.source: Jordano (2009); WBEZ (2024); Rogers Park/West Ridge Historical Society
claims.uncertainty: No post-1965 systematic count exists; persistence is documented qualitatively, not quantitatively.

entities.name: Coordinating Council of Community Organizations (CCCO)
entities.description: Chicago-based coalition that emerged in 1962 and partnered with SCLC to form the Chicago Freedom Movement. Headquartered at 366 E. 47th Street (the Wells Building). Convenor Al Raby. Dissolved late 1967.

claims.claim: The CCCO was a coalition of local civil rights groups, community groups, and church groups that had protested Chicago's segregated schools; it partnered with SCLC to launch the Chicago Freedom Movement and dissolved in late 1967.
claims.evidence: Middlebury CCCO page (citing Encyclopedia of Chicago): coalition included Chicago CORE, Chicago Area Friends of SNCC, Chicago Catholic Interracial Council, and the Chicago Urban League; headed by Al Raby by 1964; dissolved fall 1967 after Raby resigned. Indiana Law Review (Vol. 41): CFM was the collaboration of CCCO and SCLC.
claims.source: sites.middlebury.edu/chicagofreedommovement/coordinating-council-of-community-organizations/; Indiana Law Review Vol. 41
claims.uncertainty: Encyclopedia of Chicago is authoritative for the coalition composition; church-group participation is documented at the coalition level, not as specific congregations.

claims.claim: The CCCO's headquarters at 366 E. 47th Street served as a command post of the Chicago Freedom Movement.
claims.evidence: Chicago Freedom Movement sites project (Middlebury).
claims.source: sites.middlebury.edu/chicagofreedommovement/chicago-freedom-movement-sites/
claims.uncertainty: Single source for the address.

claims.claim: Brazier co-founded the CCCO with Bill Berry of the Chicago Urban League to fight segregation in Chicago's public schools; he resigned in 1965 and supported the 1966 King campaign through Al Raby.
claims.evidence: With Bill Berry of the Chicago Urban League, Brazier also formed the Coordinating Council of Community Organizations which fought segregation in Chicago's public schools; he resigned in 1965, but was active with Al Raby in Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.'s visit to Chicago in 1966. (HistoryMakers)
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A2005_003) (primary)
claims.uncertainty: Low-moderate; precise circumstances of the 1965 resignation not detailed in the finding aid.

entities.name: Deaconess Boards
entities.description: Women's board assisting with ordinances, pastoral support, and care of the needy and of women members.

claims.claim: Deaconess boards assist with church ordinances, support the clergy, minister to the needy, and educate female church members.
claims.evidence: Gilkes (1997) notes the Church Mother's career typically includes service 'in the missionary unit or on the deaconess board.' Contemporary auxiliary descriptions (e.g., Mount Olive Missionary Baptist auxiliary list) enumerate deaconess responsibilities: ordinances, clergy support, ministry to the needy, education of women members.
claims.source: Gilkes (1997); congregational auxiliary descriptions
claims.uncertainty: Specific enumerated duties come from a single contemporary congregation's public auxiliary list, not a historical or Chicago-specific source; the general existence of deaconess boards in Black churches is well attested.

entities.name: Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church
entities.description: Missionary Baptist congregation at 4501 S. Vincennes Ave., Chicago (Grand Boulevard/Bronzeville). Congregation formed 1902; since 1921 housed in the 1899 Dankmar Adler-designed Isaiah Temple synagogue; a second claimant (with Pilgrim) to the birthplace of modern gospel music — Dorsey, Theodore Frye, and Roberta Martin organized its pioneering gospel choir in 1931; Chicago Landmark and National Register (2016).

claims.claim: The Ebenezer Missionary Baptist congregation was formed in 1902; in 1921 it purchased the Isaiah Temple synagogue building at 4501 S. Vincennes Ave. — built 1898-1899 in Classical Revival style by architect Dankmar Adler (his last design), with a 1,200-seat auditorium noted for its acoustics.
claims.evidence: Chicago Landmark designation report (Dept. of Housing and Economic Development, June 2011); NPS National Register nomination; Wikipedia.
claims.source: City of Chicago, 'Landmark Designation Report: Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church' (June 2011, chicago.gov); NPS NRHP registration form.
claims.uncertainty: The 1902 formation date and 1921 purchase are the congregation's/landmark report's account; no conflicting date found.

claims.claim: The first modern gospel choir was formed at Ebenezer in 1931 under Thomas A. Dorsey, Theodore R. Frye, and Roberta Martin, blending Christian praise and blues; the choir launched the careers of Mahalia Jackson, Sallie Martin, and Dinah Washington; rock-and-roll pioneer Bo Diddley performed in the church's orchestra.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia (citing the landmark report); architecture writer John P. Walsh's account of the church.
claims.source: Wikipedia 'Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church (Chicago)'; johnpwalshblog.com (2023).
claims.uncertainty: This claim directly overlaps Pilgrim Baptist's claim that Dorsey organized the Pilgrim Gospel Chorus in 1931. Both rest on secondary accounts; the music-historical consensus places Dorsey's first choir work at Ebenezer in 1931 before his Pilgrim directorship (~1932), but that sequencing was not verified from primary records in this research.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Pilgrim Baptist's Congressional-tribute claim of a 1931 Dorsey-organized Pilgrim Gospel Chorus.

claims.claim: Listed on the National Register of Historic Places on October 24, 2016 (NRIS #16000734); designated a Chicago Landmark.
claims.evidence: NPS National Register records; Wikipedia infobox; mapcarta heritage listing.
claims.source: National Park Service, NRHP (#16000734); City of Chicago Landmarks records.
claims.uncertainty: None.

claims.claim: Ebenezer Baptist Church in Chicago was the church base where Dorsey and Frye directed the junior choir that incubated the Roberta Martin Singers.
claims.contradictory_evidence: WGN (2026) calls Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church in Bronzeville 'the birthplace of gospel music' in an anniversary story — potentially conflating or a separate claim needing verification.
claims.evidence: Smithsonian NMAH AC-0408 program notes: Roberta Martin's first church position was pianist for the Young People's Choir of Ebenezer Baptist Church; Dorsey and Frye directed it. Wikipedia: 'Theodore Frye and Thomas A. Dorsey were directing a junior choir at Ebenezer Baptist Church in Chicago, Illinois, and asked Martin to serve as the accompanist.'
claims.source: Smithsonian NMAH Archives AC-0408; Wikipedia
claims.uncertainty: Exact Ebenezer street address and its institutional relationship to the Ebenezer Missionary Baptist Church celebrated by WGN as the 'birthplace of gospel music' could not be resolved from these sources — do not conflate without verification.

Source mixes an institutional/finding-aid reference with Wikipedia or weak components; "primary" is reserved for primary records directly consulted and establishing the fact. entities.name: Elder Lucy Smith
entities.description: Founder of All Nations Pentecostal Church; Georgia-born migrant (arrived Chicago 1910) who built a nationally noted Pentecostal healing ministry led by a Black woman.

claims.claim: Lucy Smith's funeral (1952) was attended by 60,000 people, reported as the largest funeral held in Chicago up to that date.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; the figure is widely repeated but its original source is not identified in the materials accessed.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Elder Lucy Smith.'
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Elder Lucy Smith'
claims.uncertainty: Single tertiary source; attendance figure unverified against contemporary press (e.g., Chicago Defender coverage not checked).

entities.name: Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church
entities.description: Missionary Baptist congregation at 4543 S. Princeton Ave., Chicago (Washington Park/Bronzeville edge). Founded by Rev. Clay Evans (1950, disputed vs. 1958); nicknamed 'The Ship'; famed for broadcast ministry and best-selling gospel choir recordings; a civil-rights movement hub — Evans ordained Jesse Jackson and co-founded Operation PUSH.

claims.claim: Founded by Rev. Clay Evans in 1950 — Wikipedia and the Congressional Record give September 10, 1950, with five founding members; the church was earlier named Hickory Grove Baptist Church, then Mt. Carmel, before being rechristened Fellowship Baptist Church ('The Ship').
claims.evidence: Wikipedia 'Clay Evans (pastor)' and the Congressional Record tribute (Rep. Davis, Dec. 2019) both give 1950; a gospel-history account gives the earlier-name sequence (Hickory Grove → Mt. Carmel → Fellowship).
claims.source: Wikipedia 'Clay Evans (pastor)'; U.S. Congressional Record, vol. 165 (Dec. 2019), tribute to Rev. Clay Evans (Rep. Danny K. Davis); YouTube gospel-history description.
claims.uncertainty: Some biographies (e.g., Boropulse/Fortress Press biography coverage; a YouTube biography) give 1958 as the founding year, possibly confusing the Fellowship name adoption with the ministry's 1950 start. The 1950 date has the stronger attestation (Congressional Record + encyclopedia), but the conflict is real.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Biographical sources giving 1958 vs. 1950 in the Congressional Record and Wikipedia.

Source mixes an institutional/finding-aid reference with Wikipedia or weak components; "primary" is reserved for primary records directly consulted and establishing the fact. claims.claim: Church located at 4543 S. Princeton Ave., Chicago, IL 60609.
claims.evidence: The church's own website (fellowshipchicago.com); the Final Call's December 2019 coverage of Evans's death gives the same address.
claims.source: fellowshipchicago.com; The Final Call (2019-12-04).
claims.uncertainty: None on the address; the date the congregation moved to this site was not established.

claims.claim: Rev. Evans ordained the Rev. Jesse Jackson in 1968; Evans and Jackson founded Operation PUSH in 1971, with Evans as founding national board chairman (chairman 1971-1976, then chairman emeritus); Evans defied Mayor Richard J. Daley by welcoming Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. to his church during the Chicago Freedom Movement.

entities.name: Fr. George H. Clements
entities.description: Catholic priest; second African American ordained in the Archdiocese of Chicago (1957); first Black pastor of Holy Angels Catholic Church, Bronzeville (1969-1991); civil rights marcher; founder of One Church-One Child and the first U.S. Catholic priest to adopt a child (1981).

claims.claim: Clements was the second African American priest ordained in the Archdiocese of Chicago (1957) and became the first Black pastor of Holy Angels Catholic Church in Bronzeville in 1969, serving there until 1991.
claims.evidence: the second African American priest ordained in the Archdiocese of Chicago in 1957... claims.source: Religion News Service; CatholicPhilly
claims.uncertainty: Low-moderate. The 'first priest to adopt' and 170,000-children figures are widely reported; HistoryMakers gives a lower figure (100,000+), suggesting the number grew over time. Treat exact placement counts as approximate.

claims.contradictory_evidence: Archdiocese Independent Review Board found one accusation not credible (ABC7, 2022); Clements denied the 2019 accusation as 'totally unfounded.'

entities.description: Church-anchored voter registration campaign preceding Harold Washington's 1983 mayoral run. Washington said he would not run unless 50,000 new Black voters were registered; churches delivered far more.

claims.contradictory_evidence: Figure variance: ~140,000 (Christianity Today) vs. 100,000 via PUSH (Chicago Reporter, 2019).

entities.name: Liberty Baptist Church

claims.claim: Founded 1919, originating September 26, 1917, when Mrs. Bertie Boone and Mrs. Maggie Walker formed the Olive Leaf Club (a religious social club) in Boone's home at 3732 S. Federal St.; Rev. D.W. Bowen was the first pastor; the congregation later merged with two other churches.

claims.contradictory_evidence: Lynn Becker, 'Dr. King and the Story of Liberty Baptist Church' (lynnbecker.com), implies a 1918 founding vs. the church's 1919.

claims.claim: In 1924 the church purchased the Olivet Building, designed by J.M. Higginbotham (identified as one of America's first African-American architects); in 1925 Rev. D.Z. claims.uncertainty: Membership figures differ slightly between sources (3,000 vs. 2,000); Higginbotham's 'first Black architect' status is Becker's characterization.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Minor numeric variance on peak membership under Jackson.

claims.uncertainty: Timeline figures come from a single secondary narrative; corroboration from period Defender coverage would strengthen it.

claims.claim: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. chose Liberty Baptist as his headquarters when he came to Chicago in 1966 for the Chicago Freedom Movement.

claims.uncertainty: Some sources say she joined the Johnson Gospel Singers (sons of the Greater Salem pastor) at the church. Her exact Greater Salem membership tenure end date not established.

Reason: Multi-part biographical claim rests on SoulWalking (fan site) + Fandom/Wikipedia-derived page; NMAAHC confirms only part. Tertiary/weak sources. Source cited: soulwalking.co.uk; folksongindex.fandom.com (citing biography); NMAAHC

claims.claim: Jackson recorded for Decca in 1937 (first gospel artist signed to the label per some accounts) and broke through with 'Move On Up a Little Higher' (Apollo, 1947), among the highest-selling gospel singles.
claims.evidence: SoulWalking: 1937 Decca sessions, 'first gospel artist signed to the label.' Face2Face Africa/BlackAmericaWeb: 'Move On Up a Little Higher' (1947) sold millions, highest-selling gospel single; added to Library of Congress National Recording Registry (2005).
claims.source: soulwalking.co.uk; face2faceafrica.com; blackamericaweb.com
claims.uncertainty: 'First gospel artist signed to Decca' is asserted by a fan biography and should be treated as provisional.

entities.name: Metropolitan Apostolic Community Church
entities.description: Apostolic congregation at 4100 S. King Drive, Chicago (Grand Boulevard/Bronzeville), led by Rev. Dr. Leon D. Finney Jr. Occupies a landmark building with a deep civic history: its predecessor, the interracial/nonsectarian Metropolitan Community Church (1920), hosted Ida B. Wells-Barnett, Robert S. Abbott, Gwendolyn Brooks, the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters, and Eleanor Roosevelt.

claims.claim: Predecessor congregation: The Peoples Community Church of Christ and Metropolitan Community Center — later the Metropolitan Community Church — was founded in 1920 by Rev. William Decatur Cook, former pastor of Chicago's Bethel AME Church, who led over 500 followers; Cook's church purchased the 4100 S. King Drive building in 1927 after the Presbyterian congregation sold it to move to Woodlawn.
claims.evidence: Chicago Landmark designation report text for the Metropolitan Apostolic Community Church Building (reproduced online).
claims.source: City of Chicago Landmark Designation Report, 'Metropolitan Apostolic Community Church Building' (via zlibrary mirror of report PDF), accessed 2026-09-28.
claims.publication_date: report date not visible in excerpt; accessed 2026-09-28
claims.uncertainty: The report appears to be the genuine Chicago landmark document, but it was accessed via a third-party mirror; the official chicago.gov PDF should be consulted directly to confirm.

claims.claim: The Metropolitan Community Church's credo was 'Non-Sectarian, Broadly Humanitarian, Serving All The People'; its membership included journalist-activist Ida B. Wells-Barnett, Chicago Defender founder Robert S. Abbott, and poet Gwendolyn Brooks; it served as organizational home to African-American labor unions and social clubs and a venue for civil-rights activity — notably, A. Philip Randolph's Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters met there regularly, and First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt used the pulpit to speak against racial segregation of military troops during World War II.
claims.evidence: Chicago Landmark designation report text.
claims.source: City of Chicago Landmark Designation Report, 'Metropolitan Apostolic Community Church Building.'
claims.uncertainty: Same mirror-source caveat as above; these are the landmark report's historical findings, which themselves rest on archival research not re-verified here.

claims.claim: In 2003 the building was purchased by Rev. Leon Finney Jr. and the congregation of Christ Apostolic Church; out of deference to the Metropolitan's history, the congregation renamed itself the Metropolitan Apostolic Community Church.
claims.evidence: Chicago Landmark designation report text; current directory listings name Rev. Dr. Leon D. Finney Jr. as church leader at 4100 S. King Drive.
claims.source: City of Chicago Landmark Designation Report; churchesinchicago.com directory listing.
claims.uncertainty: 2003 purchase/rename per the landmark report; current leadership confirmed by directory listings.

entities.name: Missionary Societies
entities.description: Women's church auxiliaries combining evangelism, teacher training, and community uplift; the organizational base for women's religious labor in small congregations.

claims.claim: Missionary societies trained women as Sunday school teachers and community 'othermothers' who supervised children, resisted oppression, and engaged in political activism; National Baptist Convention leadership courses included educational psychology, pedagogy, child/adolescent development, and vocational guidance.
claims.evidence: P. Haggler, 'The Exact Synonym for "Missionary" is "Negro Teacher"' (peer-reviewed journal article): NBC, Inc. Sunday School Publishing Board 'National Baptist Standard Leadership Training Course' certificates were accredited by the International Council of Religious Education; missionary-society-trained teachers were expected to serve their communities as othermothers.
claims.publication_date: article date not confirmed in excerpt
claims.source: P. Haggler journal article (full citation to be confirmed -- see gaps)
claims.uncertainty: Accessed via search excerpt only; full bibliographic details and date not yet confirmed. Claim about NBC curriculum specifics rests on this single source.

entities.name: Morning Star Baptist Church
entities.description: Baptist congregation whose choir served as the training ground for the Barrett Sisters; documented example of church choirs as gospel career pipelines.

claims.claim: Morning Star Baptist Church's choir nurtured the Barrett sisters (DeLois, Billie, Rodessa), who sang there as children in the 1930s; as a high school student DeLois was recruited into the Roberta Martin Singers, and the sisters formed the Barrett Sisters in 1950.
claims.evidence: City of Chicago landmark designation report: 'They were nurtured in the choir at Morning Star Baptist Church and throughout their career returned to perform at the church' (citing Ebony, May 1988); 'As a high school student, eldest sister DeLois Barrett Campbell was recruited by the Roberta Martin Singers... The Barrett Sisters formed their own group in 1950.'
claims.source: City of Chicago Landmark Designation Report, Morning Star Baptist Church (chicago.gov)
claims.uncertainty: Municipal designation report is a primary planning document citing Ebony (1988) as its source for the music history.

entities.name: Mosque Maryam (NOI)
entities.description: Nation of Islam national headquarters in South Shore, Chicago; converted Greek Orthodox church; adjacent K-12 school.

claims.claim: Mosque Maryam (also Muhammad Mosque #2 / Temple #2) at 7351 S. Stony Island Avenue, South Shore, is the headquarters and National Center of the Nation of Islam; the building was originally the Saints Constantine and Helen Greek Orthodox Church (relocated to Palos Hills), purchased by Elijah Muhammad in 1972 and repurchased by Louis Farrakhan in 1988; named after Mary, mother of Jesus ('Maryam' is Arabic for Mary).
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found on location or purchase dates; the $3 million Gaddafi loan is reported as Farrakhan's statement, not independently verified.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Mosque Maryam': purchase 1972 by Elijah Muhammad; repurchase 1988 by Farrakhan; name origin; adjacent Muhammad University of Islam (pre-K-12). Farrakhan's Gaddafi-loan statement also reported there.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Mosque Maryam'
claims.uncertainty: Tertiary source; the 1972/1988 transaction dates and the Gaddafi loan claim need corroboration from NOI publications or press archives.

claims.claim: Mosque Maryam serves as NOI headquarters with Farrakhan's offices on the premises, and the adjacent Muhammad University of Islam educates boys and girls from preschool through 12th grade.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia, 'Mosque Maryam.'
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Mosque Maryam'
claims.uncertainty: Tertiary source; institutional role is consistent with NOI's public self-presentation.

entities.name: Mother Consuella York
entities.description: Baptist woman minister ordained by Rev. Clay Evans; described by Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church and community press as the first Black woman ordained into the Baptist clergy in Chicago; later presided over a church.

claims.claim: Mother Consuella York was the first Black woman ordained into the Baptist clergy in Chicago, ordained by Rev. Clay Evans.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located, but absence of a denominational or newspaper record of the ordination itself keeps this Provisional.
claims.evidence: Reverend Dr. Clay Evans has been responsible for launching the ministerial careers of ninety-three people, including Mother Consuella York, the first female to be ordained in the Baptist Denomination in Chicago. (church site); 'the first Black woman to be ordained into the Baptist clergy in the city of Chicago' (Final Call, quoting Rev. Janette Wilson)
claims.source: Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church official site (primary); The Final Call, Dec 2019 (secondary)
claims.uncertainty: Moderate-high. The 'first' claim is repeated by the ordaining church and community press but is difficult to verify exhaustively; the year (1954 per Rev. Wilson in the Final Call) comes from a single quoted source and the church's own site gives no date. No denominational ordination record was located in this pass.

claims.claim: After ordination, Mother York presided over a church -- described as an unprecedented step for a woman in Chicago's Baptist world.
claims.evidence: It was an unprecedented and bold move for a woman to not only speak from a church pulpit but to preside over a church.
claims.source: The Final Call, Dec 2019 (quoting Rev. Janette Wilson)
claims.uncertainty: High. The identity of the church she presided over, its dates, and any public civic role she played beyond ordination were not located in this pass.

entities.name: Muhammad's Temple No. 2 (NOI)
entities.description: The Nation of Islam's Chicago mosque/temple (1932- ), predecessor institution to Mosque Maryam; documented at multiple South Side addresses.

claims.claim: The Nation of Islam's Temple No. 2 was founded in Chicago in 1932 by Elijah Muhammad.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; consistent with NOI's own period statement ('The movement in Chicago was founded in 1932 by Elijah Mohammed').
claims.evidence: Encyclopedia.com entry on Elijah Muhammad: 'established Southside Mosque in Chicago, IL, 1932.' NOI handbill scan (docs.wixstatic.com PDF): 'The movement in Chicago was founded in 1932 by Elijah Mohammed.' Curtis (2016), via sci-hub excerpt: after Fard's 1934 departure, Elijah Muhammad 'established his headquarters in Chicago at the Nation of Islam's Temple No. 2.'
claims.source: Encyclopedia.com; NOI period handbill; Edward E. Curtis IV (2016) via excerpt
claims.uncertainty: Encyclopedia.com is tertiary; the NOI handbill is a primary document but accessed as an unauthenticated scan. Founding year consistent across sources.

claims.claim: Temple No. 2 occupied successive South Side locations: 824 E. 43rd Street (advertised meetings, undated handbill); 5335 S. Greenwood Avenue with the University of Islam at 5883 S. Greenwood (FBI-file summary, c. 1960s); then the Stony Island building (1972).
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; the address sequence is inferred from documents of different dates, not from a single institutional history.
claims.evidence: NOI handbill: 'The Holy Temple of Islam NO.2, 824 E. 43rd Street Chicago 15, Illinois. Meetings every Wednesday and Friday 8 P.M. and Sunday 2 P.M.' FBI-file summary (upload.wikimedia.org): 'Muhammad's Mosque No. 2, is located at 5335 South Greenwood Avenue, and adjacent to it is the University of Islam... at 5883 South Greenwood.'
claims.publication_date: handbill undated (mid-20th c.); FBI summary c. 1960s
claims.source: NOI handbill scan; FBI file summary
claims.uncertainty: Handbill is undated and accessed as an unauthenticated web scan; FBI file is a government surveillance document with its own biases and possible inaccuracies. Address chronology is reconstructed, not stated by the institution.

entities.name: National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses
entities.description: Annual convention co-founded by Thomas A. Dorsey and Sallie Martin (1932/1933) to organize gospel choirs; also known as the Dorsey Convention; still active.

claims.claim: Dorsey and Sallie Martin co-founded the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses (NCGCC); sources commonly date it to 1933.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Word in Black (2024) and Wikipedia date the founding to 1932 via the Gospel Choral Union of Chicago; BlackPast and Path MEGAzine date NCGCC to 1933.
claims.evidence: BlackPast: 'With him, in 1933, Martin co-founded the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses.' Path MEGAzine: Dorsey 'founded the National Convention of Gospel Choirs and Choruses (NCGCC) in 1933.' NCGCC continues operating (91st session in 2024 per Word in Black/NNPA).
claims.source: BlackPast.org (Janet Hauck); Path MEGAzine (2017); Word in Black/NNPA (2024)
claims.uncertainty: Founding year is inconsistently reported: 1933 (BlackPast, Path MEGAzine) vs. 1932 (Word in Black 2024: 'led the convention from its founding in 1932'; Wikipedia's Dorsey article: 'In 1932 however... Dorsey co-founded the Gospel Choral Union of Chicago – eventually renamed the NCGCC'). The 1932/1933 split may reflect the Gospel Choral Union of Chicago's founding (1932) vs. the NCGCC naming/reorganization (1933). Red-team harmonization (2026-09-28): founding year disputed 1932 vs 1933; NCGCC incorporation records needed.

claims.claim: The NCGCC was organized to unify gospel choirs into a collective body with annual sessions of classes, workshops, and concerts.
claims.evidence: Path MEGAzine: Dorsey 'recognized a need to organize gospel choirs collectively into unions... first convention of its kind.' Word in Black (2024): the convention offers sessions for youth and adults 'to enhance their skills as singers, instrumentalists, educators and leaders' and showcases newly written gospel music.
claims.source: Path MEGAzine (2017); Word in Black/NNPA (2024)
claims.uncertainty: None on purpose; exact original charter language not retrieved.

entities.name: New Friendship Baptist Church
entities.description: 854 W. 71st Street, Englewood. Pastor Rev. Stroy Freeman. Served as the first major staging area for Chicago Freedom Movement rallies and marches on the South Side.

claims.claim: New Friendship Baptist served as the first major staging area for Chicago Freedom Movement rallies and marches on the South Side; Rev. Stroy Freeman had helped lead a 1962 Chicago delegation to Albany, Georgia, and was an early supporter of Operation Breadbasket.
claims.evidence: Chicago Freedom Movement sites project (Middlebury).
claims.source: sites.middlebury.edu/chicagofreedommovement/chicago-freedom-movement-sites/
claims.uncertainty: Single scholarly-curated source; corroboration from Defender or SCLC records needed.

claims.claim: Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his 'My place is in Gage Park' speech at New Friendship Baptist Church on August 4, 1966.
claims.evidence: Chicago Freedom Movement sites project (Middlebury). Consistent with the July 1966 Gage Park marches staged from the church.
claims.source: sites.middlebury.edu/chicagofreedommovement/chicago-freedom-movement-sites/
claims.uncertainty: Date and venue from a single curated source; SCLC papers or contemporary press would confirm.

claims.claim: On July 29, 1966, roughly 450 marchers led by Andrew Young, Al Raby, and other lieutenants marched from New Friendship Baptist to H.F. Halverson Realty at 63rd and Kedzie in Gage Park.
claims.evidence: Harold Titus blog summarizing David Bernstein's account of the Chicago Freedom Movement (citing Bernstein).
claims.source: Harold Titus blog (goodreads.com), citing Bernstein
claims.uncertainty: Blog summary of a secondary account; needs confirmation from Defender or SCLC records.

entities.name: Olivet Baptist Church
entities.description: Baptist congregation at 3101 S. King Drive, Chicago (Douglas/Bronzeville). Formed 1861 (disputed vs. 1850) by the merger of Zoar and Mt. Zion Baptist churches; oldest operating African-American Baptist church in Chicago; famed for Great Migration-era social services and gospel influence; at its peak claimed as the largest Protestant congregation in the world.

claims.claim: On December 22, 1861, Rev. J.F. (Jesse Freeman) Boulden and Rev. Tansbury combined Zoar Baptist Church and Mt. Zion Baptist Church to form Olivet Baptist Church under Boulden's leadership; Boulden served until 1863, followed by Rev. Richard DeBaptiste (1863-1882).
claims.evidence: Church's own history page (olivetchicago.org) and encyclopedic accounts agree on the December 22, 1861 union date and Boulden/DeBaptiste succession.
claims.source: Olivet Baptist Church, 'History' (olivetchicago.org); Wikipedia 'Olivet Baptist Church' (citing association minutes and histories).
claims.publication_date: church page accessed 2026-09-28; Wikipedia article current as of 2026
claims.uncertainty: The 1861 merger date is well attested; see dispute below on the congregation's claimed 1850 origin.

contradiction_noted.subject: Olivet Baptist Church 1861 formation — grade spread
contradiction_noted.guidance: Substantively compatible (1850 predecessor vs 1861 merger); do not silently harmonize grades. Present the grade spread.

red_team_notes: Cross-project audit 2026-09-28: contradiction-noted (Medium). Olivet Baptist Church 1861 formation — grade spread. See also: CTL-DR-BCI-001/b-olivet, CTL-DR-BVM-005/church-olivet. Substantively compatible (1850 predecessor vs 1861 merger); do not silently harmonize grades. Present the grade spread.

Cross-project audit 2026-09-28: source_type primary -> secondary. Source mixes an institutional/finding-aid reference with Wikipedia or weak components; "primary" is reserved for primary records directly consulted and establishing the fact. Source: Olivet Baptist Church, 'History' (olivetchicago.org); Wikipedia 'Olivet Baptist Church' (citing association mi

claims.claim: The congregation traces its own origin to April 6, 1850, when it was organized as Xenia Baptist Church (3 members), renamed Zoar Baptist Church on April 6, 1853 — i.e., the church claims an 1850 founding, while most external sources date Olivet to the 1861 merger.
claims.evidence: The church's own history page explicitly gives the 1850 Xenia organization and 1853 Zoar renaming; encyclopedic sources consistently give 1861.
claims.source: Olivet Baptist Church, 'History' (olivetchicago.org) vs. Wikipedia/encyclopedic sources.
claims.uncertainty: Classic anniversary-history vs. external-record conflict: the church counts its predecessor congregation's 1850 organization; external sources date the Olivet name to 1861. Both dates are defensible on different definitions of 'founding.'
claims.contradictory_evidence: Church's own claim (1850/1853) vs. Wikipedia, NPS-referenced histories (1861).
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit 2026-09-28: source_type primary -> secondary. Source mixes an institutional/finding-aid reference with Wikipedia or weak components; "primary" is reserved for primary records directly consulted and establishing the fact. Source: Olivet Baptist Church, 'History' (olivetchicago.org) vs. Wikipedia/encyclopedic sources.

claims.claim: Oldest operating African-American Baptist church in Chicago.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedic sources state this; consistent with the 1861 (or 1850) origin.
claims.source: Wikipedia 'Olivet Baptist Church,' accessed 2026-09-28.
claims.uncertainty: No competing older Black Baptist congregation identified, but the claim rests on encyclopedic synthesis, not a comparative survey of records.

claims.claim: Membership grew to about 11,000 in the 1920s and about 20,000 by the 1940s, making it the largest African-American church in the United States and, at its heyday, the largest Protestant congregation in the world.
claims.evidence: Encyclopedic accounts; the church's own history says under Dr. Lacey Kirk Williams (pastor from 1916) Olivet 'became known as the largest Protestant congregation in the world.'
claims.source: Wikipedia 'Olivet Baptist Church'; olivetchicago.org history page.
claims.uncertainty: Membership figures are rounded estimates repeated across secondary sources; no primary membership rolls consulted. 'Largest in the world' is a superlative that cannot be independently verified without comparative data.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found on the order of magnitude; the superlative is unverified.

claims.claim: Under Dr. Lacey (Lacy) Kirk Williams, called to the pastorate in 1916 during the first Great Migration, Olivet built a social-service infrastructure for Southern migrants — assistance finding housing and childcare, and Chicago's first kindergarten program — described by Princeton professor Wallace Best as a 'national model' for migrant settlement ministry.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia account citing religious-studies scholarship; church's own history credits Williams with leading Olivet to national/international prominence and the presidency of the National Baptist Convention USA.
claims.source: Wikipedia 'Olivet Baptist Church' (citing Wallace Best); olivetchicago.org history page.
claims.uncertainty: 'First kindergarten in Chicago' is a strong claim needing a primary-source check; Wallace Best's characterization is scholarly but secondhand here.

claims.claim: Current location: 3101 S. King Drive (Martin Luther King Jr. Drive), Chicago, Douglas community area.
claims.evidence: OpenStreetMap/Wikidata-derived listings and the church's own site identify the 3101 S. King Drive address.
claims.source: mapcarta.com/Olivet Baptist Church entry; olivetchicago.org.
claims.uncertainty: Address confirmed by multiple listings; the date of the move to this site was not established in this research.

claims.claim: Under Rev. Lacy Kirk Williams (pastor from 1916), Olivet directed arriving migrants toward housing, offered daycare, and created a kindergarten program described by its current pastor as the city's first.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found, but the superlative ('first') is unverified.
claims.evidence: Pastor John L. Smith interview: 'When Black migrants arrived, the church directed them toward housing, offered day care and created the city's first kindergarten program.' Princeton professor Wallace Best quoted calling Olivet a national model for churches bridging the gap to help Black migrants settle.
claims.source: Afro-Conscious Media, 'How Chicago's Olivet Baptist Church welcomed Black migrants during the Great Migration,' April 4, 2026
claims.uncertainty: The 'city's first kindergarten' claim rests on a single interview with the current pastor; no independent or archival corroboration found in this research.

claims.claim: Northern Black churches, with Chicago as the detailed case study, provided food, clothing, housing, educational, health, leisure, and employment services to migrants and their families during the Great Migration.
claims.evidence: Milton Sernett's 'Bound for the Promised Land' uses Chicago as a detailed case study showing mainline Black Baptist and AME churches responding to migrants' spiritual and material needs; describes migrant reception as a 'special mission' and 'sacred duty.'
claims.source: Milton C. Sernett, 'Bound for the Promised Land: African American Religion and the Great Migration' (Duke University Press, 1997), as summarized in review
claims.uncertainty: General pattern is well supported; specific Olivet program details still rely on congregational memory.

claims.claim: In 1918 Olivet Baptist purchased the Gothic Revival church at 3101 S. King Drive from the First Baptist Church of Chicago for $80,000.
claims.evidence: Preservation Chicago: First Baptist sold the building to Olivet for $80,000 as the Douglas neighborhood became almost entirely Black; transaction described as 'one of the greatest examples of a Baptist Missionary endeavor in the city.' Second Preservation Chicago page confirms 1918 purchase of the 1876 Wilcox and Miller building.
claims.source: Preservation Chicago, 'Olivet Baptist Church' and 'Olivet Baptist Church Proposed as Centerpiece of Large Mixed-Use Development (Chicago 7 2025)'
claims.uncertainty: Both citations come from the same preservation organization; deed records would provide primary confirmation.

claims.claim: In 2025 Olivet proposed Trinity Square, an estimated $157 million mixed-use development with 366 mixed-income apartments (80% affordable), plus a podium with daycare, food pantry, workforce development incubator, and health and wellness clinic, on church property adjacent to 3101 S. King Drive.
claims.evidence: Chicago Sun-Times reporting (Mariah Rush, 4/29/25) and Urbanize Chicago (4/20/25): 28-29 story tower, 366 units, no more than 20% market-rate, 10% set aside for tenants with no income; developer partnership with Crossing Capital Group of New Jersey; listed on Preservation Chicago's 2025 Chicago 7 Most Endangered.
claims.source: Urbanize Chicago, 'Mixed-use development planned around Olivet Baptist Church,' April 20, 2025; Chicago Sun-Times, April 29, 2025
claims.uncertainty: Announced plans; city approval and financing not confirmed in sources found.

claims.claim: Jackson pastored Olivet from 1941 to 1990, growing membership from approximately 10,000 to more than 20,000.
claims.evidence: In 1941, Jackson was called to pastor the historic Olivet Baptist Church on Chicago's South Side, where he served until his death in 1990. During his close to fifty year leadership at Olivet Baptist Church the membership in the congregation grew from approximately 10,000 to more than 20,000.
claims.source: Wikipedia (Joseph H. Jackson), citing denominational sources
claims.uncertainty: Moderate. Encyclopedia figures; no congregational roll or denominational audit located in this pass.

entities.name: Operation Breadbasket
entities.description: SCLC's economic-justice arm, launched in Chicago in 1966 under Jesse Jackson's leadership; developed out of weekly meetings at Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church; ultimately became the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition.

claims.claim: Operation Breadbasket developed out of early weekly meetings at Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church under Jesse Jackson as associate pastor, and ultimately became the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition.
claims.evidence: Chicago Freedom Movement sites project (Middlebury): 'Jesse Jackson was an associate pastor, and he oversaw the development of Operation Breadbasket which ultimately became Rainbow/PUSH Coalition.'
claims.source: sites.middlebury.edu/chicagofreedommovement/chicago-freedom-movement-sites/
claims.uncertainty: Well-established organizational lineage; the specific meeting-venue claim relies on the Middlebury site.

entities.name: Operation PUSH / Rainbow PUSH Coalition
entities.description: Chicago-founded civil rights organization: Operation Breadbasket (SCLC economic arm, 1962) -> Operation PUSH (founded by Jesse Jackson, Dec 1971) -> National Rainbow Coalition (mid-1980s) -> merged as Rainbow PUSH Coalition (1996). Clergy-led throughout: Clay Evans (founding board chair), Willie Barrow (executive director/chair/CEO), Addie Wyatt (board).

claims.claim: Operation PUSH was founded in Chicago in December 1971 by Rev. Jesse Jackson after his break with the SCLC; it merged with the National Rainbow Coalition in 1996 to form the Rainbow PUSH Coalition.
claims.evidence: December 1971 - Resigns from the SCLC and forms Operation PUSH (People United to Save Humanity) in Chicago. (CNN); September 1996 - Operation PUSH and the Rainbow Coalition merge to form Rainbow PUSH Coalition. (CNN)
claims.source: CNN Fast Facts: Jesse Jackson (secondary)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Clergy held its top posts: Clay Evans was founding national board chairman (1971-1976), Willie Barrow succeeded Jackson as executive director (1984) and later chaired the board as CEO, and Addie Wyatt served on the PUSH board.
claims.evidence: Founding National Board Chairman of the Rainbow (PUSH) Coalition... (1971-1976) (Fellowship Chicago, primary); Barrow replaced Jackson as executive director of Operation PUSH in 1984 (Citizen Newspaper Group); served on the board of Operation PUSH (HistoryMakers, on Wyatt)
claims.source: Fellowship Chicago official site; Citizen Newspaper Group; The HistoryMakers
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Phyllis Wheatley Club and Home / Bethel A.M.E. Church
entities.description: Black women's club founded 1896; established the Phyllis Wheatley Home in 1908 to house Black migrant women and girls arriving without relatives or resources. Held a citywide mass meeting at Bethel A.M.E. Church on January 29, 1911, exemplifying churches as the meeting infrastructure of Black women's settlement work.

claims.claim: In January 1911 the Phyllis Wheatley Club organized a mass meeting of Black middle-class women at Bethel A.M.E. Church to raise support for the Phyllis Wheatley Home, the settlement home for migrant women it had established in 1908.
claims.evidence: Abraham Carter Kimani Sr., UCLA M.A. thesis 'Mothers of the City' (2012): 'In January 1911, the Phyllis Wheatley Club organized a "mass meeting of all the [Black middleclass] women in the city to be held at Bethel A.M.E. Church on Sunday January 29, 1911 at 3 p.m."' The Home, established 1908, housed migrant women and girls arriving without relatives or economic resources.
claims.source: Abraham Carter Kimani Sr., 'Mothers of the City: The Phyllis Wheatley Club and Home, the Great Migration, and Communal Family in Black Chicago, 1910-1930,' UCLA M.A. thesis, 2012 (escholarship.org)
claims.uncertainty: Thesis cites the Chicago Defender; the underlying primary (Defender, Jan 1911) was not directly consulted.

claims.claim: Churches conducted the bulk of Black settlement work through establishing nursery centers, mother's clubs, and kindergartens; Black clubwomen drew economic support from Black churches for this work.
claims.evidence: Kimani thesis (2012), citing scholarship on Black women's settlement work: 'Churches conducted the bulk of settlement work through establishing nursery centers, mother's clubs, and kindergartens.'
claims.source: Kimani, UCLA M.A. thesis, 2012
claims.uncertainty: Secondhand citation within a thesis; the underlying scholarship (e.g., Anne Meis Knupfer's 'Toward a Tenderer Humanity,' 1996) should be consulted directly.

entities.name: Pilgrim Baptist Church
entities.description: Baptist congregation in Bronzeville (3301 S. Indiana Ave.), founded 1916 (disputed vs. 1922). Under Rev. Junius C. Austin and music director Thomas A. Dorsey it became the celebrated 'birthplace of gospel music'; its 1891 Louis Sullivan/Dankmar Adler synagogue building was destroyed by fire in 2006 and not rebuilt.

claims.claim: Founded in September 1916 from the Union Grove Prayer Meeting Club, meeting in the home of Deacon John A. Finnie at 242 E. 42nd St.; Mrs. Juanita Finnie suggested the name 'Pilgrim Baptist Church'; Rev. Jessie D. Luck of New York became the first pastor in January 1917.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tribute by Rep. Danny K. Davis (September 10, 2013), based on the congregation's institutional history.
claims.source: U.S. Congressional Record, vol. 159 (2013-09-10), 'Pilgrim Baptist Church' tribute (Rep. Danny K. Davis).
claims.uncertainty: The 1916 date is the congregation's own claim as transmitted through a Congressional tribute; the Smithsonian NMAAHC catalogs the church as 'founded 1922' — see Disputed status below.
claims.contradictory_evidence: NMAAHC object record (nmaahc.si.edu) lists 'Pilgrim Baptist Church, American, founded 1922.'
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit harmonization 2026-09-28. H3: corpus position is "September 1916 (congregation's claim; NMAAHC catalogs 1922)" — never print 1916 bare.

claims.claim: In 1922 Pilgrim purchased the Kehilath Anshe Ma'ariv synagogue at 3301 S. Indiana Ave. — built 1890-1891 to designs by Louis Sullivan and Dankmar Adler (initial drawings by draftsman Frank Lloyd Wright).
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tribute (2013); NPR (2006); Ekklesia/BBC coverage of the 2006 fire; architectural references.
claims.source: Congressional Record vol. 159 (2013); NPR 'The Music of Pilgrim Baptist Church' (2006-01-12).
claims.uncertainty: Consistent across all sources; Sullivan/Adler attribution is uncontested.

claims.claim: In 1931 (per the Congressional tribute; 'the 1930s' per NMAAHC), Thomas A. Dorsey — 'the father of Gospel Music' — was brought to Pilgrim by Rev. Junius Caesar Austin and organized the Pilgrim Baptist Church Gospel Chorus, including singers Mahalia Jackson, Sally/Sallie Martin, Roberta Martin, and Clara Ward; Pilgrim became known as the birthplace of gospel music.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tribute (2013) gives 1931; NMAAHC piano object record says Dorsey was hired by Pastor Austin in the 1930s; NPR (2006) calls it 'the mother church of an entire genre.'
claims.source: Congressional Record vol. 159 (2013); NMAAHC object nmaahc_2015.134.1a-g; NPR (2006-01-12).
claims.uncertainty: Pilgrim's 1931 claim directly overlaps Ebenezer Missionary Baptist's own 1931 claim (first gospel choir at Ebenezer led by Dorsey, Theodore Frye, Roberta Martin). Music histories generally place Dorsey's first choir work at Ebenezer in 1931 and his move to Pilgrim's music directorship around 1932; neither date was verified from primary personnel records here.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Ebenezer's landmark/NRHP materials also claim a 1931 first gospel choir with Dorsey. The two churches' claims are in direct tension.
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit harmonization 2026-09-28. H1: this Disputed 1931 claim is now explicitly the minority/congregational-memory position; corpus position is 1932.

claims.claim: The Rev. C.L. Franklin served as assistant pastor at Pilgrim (with Rev. R.T. Schell carrying on after Rev. Watson's passing) before the call of Rev. Junius Caesar Austin.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tribute (2013) names Watson, Schell, assistant pastor C.L. Franklin, and then Austin as the sequence leading to Austin's pastorate.
claims.source: Congressional Record vol. 159 (2013).
claims.uncertainty: Single source; tenure dates not given.

claims.claim: On January 6, 2006, the historic building was destroyed by fire during a roof-repair project (a propane torch ignited the roof; workers fled and no 911 call was made in time); the congregation continued in surviving lower-level space and the landmarked ruin was not rebuilt.
claims.evidence: NPR (2006), ChicagoTalks/Columbia College reporting (2015), and Ekklesia/BBC coverage all describe the fire's cause and aftermath.
claims.source: NPR 'The Music of Pilgrim Baptist Church' (2006-01-12); chicagotalks.colum.edu (2015).
claims.uncertainty: Consistent across contemporaneous reporting; no official fire-investigation report consulted.

claims.claim: Aviator Bessie Coleman was a member of the Pilgrim congregation.
claims.evidence: NMAAHC object record lists 'Famous members of the congregation include Bessie Coleman.'
claims.source: Smithsonian NMAAHC object record nmaahc_2015.134.1a-g.
claims.uncertainty: Museum-catalog statement; primary membership records not consulted.

claims.claim: Pilgrim Baptist Church (originally built as a synagogue 1890–1891, architects Adler and Sullivan) became the home of Pilgrim Baptist in 1922 and is widely described as the birthplace of modern gospel music.
claims.contradictory_evidence: NMAAHC lists Pilgrim Baptist Church as founded 1922 vs. National Trust's 1920 occupancy of the building.
claims.evidence: National Trust: the 1891 building became Pilgrim's home in 1920 and is considered the birthplace of modern American gospel music. NMAAHC confirms the building's Adler/Sullivan synagogue origins and gospel association. Fire damaged the church in 2006.
claims.source: National Trust for Historic Preservation (Preservation, Spring 2016); NMAAHC
claims.uncertainty: The NMAAHC object caption says Pilgrim Baptist was 'founded 1922' while the National Trust says the congregation occupied the building from 1920 — possibly a discrepancy between congregation founding and building occupancy dates. Red-team harmonization (2026-09-28): corrected from 1920 to 1922 per track-a (Verified); 1920 date was erroneous.

claims.claim: Pastor Junius C. Austin hired Dorsey as music director in the 1930s; the rehearsal piano Dorsey used at Pilgrim is now held by the NMAAHC.
claims.evidence: NMAAHC object record for the Cable Piano Company piano: 'used as a rehearsal piano by music director, Thomas A. Dorsey... Hired by influential pastor Junius C. Austin in the 1930s, Dorsey helped make Pilgrim one of the largest churches in the country.'
claims.source: NMAAHC object record nmaahc_2015.134.1a-g (primary artifact cataloging)
claims.uncertainty: Museum cataloging is a primary institutional record of the object; the historical hiring narrative it contains relies on museum research, not a contemporaneous document.

claims.claim: Pilgrim's music program drew singers including Mahalia Jackson, Sallie Martin, Albertina Walker, Aretha Franklin, James Cleveland, the Staple Singers, and the Edwin Hawkins Singers.
claims.evidence: NMAAHC caption: 'Albertina Walker, Mahalia Jackson, Sallie Martin, Aretha Franklin, James Cleveland, The Staple Singers and The Edwin Hawkins singers are among those who have sung at the church.'
claims.source: NMAAHC object record nmaahc_2015.134.1a-g
claims.uncertainty: The record distinguishes those who 'sung at the church' from members of the congregation (e.g., Bessie Coleman listed as a member).

entities.name: Project Vote! 1992 (Illinois)
entities.description: Statewide voter registration drive directed in Illinois by Barack Obama. Recruited staff and volunteers from Black churches and community groups; trained 700 deputy registrars out of 11,000 citywide.

claims.claim: Obama recruited staff and volunteers from Black churches, community groups, and politicians; trained 700 deputy registrars; ran a saturation media campaign with Black-owned Brainstorm Communications ('It's a Power Thing'); minority McDonald's owners hosted registrars and donated radio time; labor unions and later the Clinton/Gore campaign (directed locally by Alderman Bobby Rush) provided funding.
claims.evidence: Chicago Magazine, 'Vote of Confidence': 'Obama... had recruited staff and volunteers from black churches, community groups, and politicians. He helped train 700 deputy registrars, out of a total of 11,000 citywide.'
claims.source: Chicago Magazine, 'Vote of Confidence'
claims.uncertainty: Retrospective magazine account; Project Vote organizational records would be primary.

entities.name: Quinn Chapel AME Church
entities.description: 2401 S. Wabash Avenue. Chicago's oldest African American congregation: origins as a seven-member prayer group in 1844, organized 1847, named for Bishop William P. Quinn. Chicago Landmark (1977); National Register of Historic Places (1979). Active in abolition and social reform.

claims.claim: Originated as a nondenominational prayer group of seven individuals in 1844, meeting in the home of John Day near State and Randolph; later moved to the home of Maria Parker and then an old schoolhouse at State and Madison.
claims.evidence: Narrated on the church's own history page, quinnchicago.org/history/.
claims.source: Quinn Chapel AME Church, 'HISTORY' (quinnchicago.org), accessed 2026-09-28.
claims.uncertainty: Single-source congregation claim; no independent antebellum record consulted.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; the 1844/1847 two-stage origin is repeated consistently across secondary sources.

contradiction_noted.subject: Quinn Chapel 1844 prayer-group origin — Verified vs Provisional
contradiction_noted.guidance: 1844 origin rests on congregational tradition; 1847 AME recognition is the Verified anchor.

red_team_notes: Cross-project audit 2026-09-28: contradiction-noted (Medium). Quinn Chapel 1844 prayer-group origin — Verified vs Provisional. See also: CTL-DR-BCI-001/b-quinn, CTL-DR-BVM-005/church-quinn-chapel. 1844 origin rests on congregational tradition; 1847 AME recognition is the Verified anchor.

claims.claim: On July 22, 1847, formally recognized as an official congregation of the African Methodist Episcopal Church and named Quinn Chapel for Bishop William Paul Quinn; Rev. George Johnson led the 1847 organization.
claims.evidence: Church's own history page gives the July 22, 1847 recognition date; the Congressional Record tribute (Rep. Danny K. Davis, c. 1997, on the church's 150th anniversary) states that in 1847 the fellowship 'formally took its name under the leadership of Rev. George Johnson' in honor of Bishop William Paul Quinn.
claims.source: Quinn Chapel AME Church 'HISTORY' (quinnchicago.org); U.S. Congressional Record, vol. 143, 'Tribute to Quinn Chapel AME Church' (Rep. Danny K. Davis), c. 1997.
claims.uncertainty: The 1847 founding is treated as the AME-recognition date; 'founded 1847' in shorthand conflates prayer-group (1844) and AME-recognition (1847) phases.

claims.claim: Quinn Chapel is Chicago's oldest African-American congregation.
claims.evidence: Repeated across the church's own materials, the National Park Service/HABS survey entry (HABS IL-1204), and encyclopedia entries.
claims.source: Historic American Buildings Survey entry for Quinn Chapel (Library of Congress); quinnchicago.org.
claims.publication_date: HABS survey material archived (undated online reproduction)
claims.uncertainty: Verified as the oldest continuously operating Black congregation; qualified by the caveat that pre-1847 Black worship groups may have existed without surviving records.

claims.claim: The church was a station on the Underground Railroad and active in Chicago's abolitionist movement before the Civil War.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tribute (Davis) and church history both state this; the 1847-era congregation was located downtown (present site of the Monadnock Building).
claims.source: Congressional Record, vol. 143, Quinn Chapel tribute, c. 1997.
claims.uncertainty: Repeated in secondary sources but no primary abolitionist-era documentation consulted; Underground Railroad claims for individual buildings are frequently difficult to verify.

claims.claim: The Great Chicago Fire of 1871 destroyed the church's original downtown building; the congregation worshipped in temporary locations for years before purchasing the present site in 1890 and building the current church (designed by Henry F.
