Starbuck, exterior; Charles H. McAfee, interior) in 1891-1892 at 2401 S. Wabash Ave.
claims.evidence: Church history page (site purchased 1890, standing at Wabash and 24th since 1891); HABS/NPS materials (Starbuck design, 1891-92 construction); Wikipedia cites Chicago Landmark records.
claims.source: quinnchicago.org; National Park Service / HABS materials; Chicago Department of Planning and Development Landmarks Division records.
claims.uncertainty: Minor: congregation says 'since 1891' vs. 'built 1892' in encyclopedic sources — consistent with design 1891/construction 1891-92.

claims.claim: Designated a Chicago Landmark on August 3, 1977, and listed on the National Register of Historic Places on September 4, 1979 (NRIS #79000827).
claims.evidence: NPS National Register Information System; City of Chicago Landmarks records.
claims.source: National Park Service, National Register of Historic Places (#79000827); City of Chicago Landmark designation, 1977.
claims.uncertainty: None.

claims.claim: Quinn Chapel was the birthplace of Provident Hospital of Chicago (organized by Dr. Daniel Hale Williams in 1891) and initiated the first retirement home for African-Americans in 1898 (Elam House).
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tribute by Rep. Davis (c. 1997) states both; church-associated histories repeat the Provident Hospital claim.
claims.source: U.S. Congressional Record, vol. 143, Quinn Chapel tribute, c. 1997.
claims.uncertainty: Government-record statement, but reflects the congregation's own anniversary claims; Provident Hospital was founded in 1891 by Dr. Williams — the Quinn Chapel connection needs corroboration from hospital founding records. The 1898 retirement home claim similarly awaits independent confirmation.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; no hospital record consulted.

claims.claim: Quinn Chapel served as a station on the Underground Railroad and supported the abolition movement; it is the oldest African American congregation in Chicago.
claims.evidence: Historic American Buildings Survey (HABS IL-1204, Library of Congress): 'An active advocate of social service and reform, the Quinn congregation served as a station on the Underground Railroad and supported the abolition movement.' Chicago Landmark designation 1977; NRHP listing 1979.
claims.source: Historic American Buildings Survey IL-1204 (Library of Congress); Friends of Historic Second Church program page
claims.uncertainty: None material; landmark and HABS documentation are authoritative. Red-team harmonization (2026-09-28): single-track verification with 'none material' uncertainty is insufficient.

claims.claim: Quinn Chapel was the birthplace of Provident Hospital of Chicago, organized by Dr. Daniel Hale Williams in 1891.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tribute by Rep. Danny Davis (1997): 'Quinn Chapel was the birthplace of Provident Hospital of Chicago, organized by Dr. Daniel Hale Williams in 1891.' HABS summary: members 'instrumental in founding such institutions as Provident Hospital, The Elam House, and The Wabash Avenue YMCA.'
claims.source: Congressional Record, Vol. 143, 'Tribute to Quinn Chapel AME Church' (Rep. Danny K. Davis, 1997)
claims.uncertainty: Planning meetings for Provident were held at Quinn Chapel; 'birthplace' is a fair characterization of the organizing site. Red-team harmonization (2026-09-28): HABS supports 'instrumental in founding' only; hospital records not consulted.

claims.claim: Quinn Chapel initiated in 1898 the first retirement home for African Americans.
claims.evidence: Congressional Record tribute (1997): 'it was Quinn Chapel who initiated in 1898 the first retirement home for African-Americans.'
claims.source: Congressional Record, Vol. 143, 'Tribute to Quinn Chapel AME Church' (Rep. Danny K. Davis, 1997)
claims.uncertainty: Single source; needs archival corroboration from church records or contemporary press.

claims.claim: The 2015 'Souls to the Polls' initiative, in which religious leaders pledged to transport at least 100 congregations to the polls for early voting in the February mayoral election, was announced at Quinn Chapel A.M.E.
claims.evidence: Medill Reports Chicago (Northwestern), Jan 31, 2015: 'Ministers and community activists across Chicago have pledged to transport at least 100 congregations to the polls for early voting on Sunday, February 15. They announced the "Souls to the Polls" initiative Wednesday at Quinn Chapel A.M.E. Church on the Near South Side.'
claims.source: Medill Reports Chicago, 'Religious leaders pledge to increase black voter turnout,' January 31, 2015
claims.uncertainty: None material.

claims.claim: Founded in 1847, Quinn Chapel is Chicago's oldest Black church (described by Stanford as the city's 'second oldest Protestant church').
claims.evidence: Founded in 1847, the spacious and prestigious Quinn Chapel AME Church was Chicago's oldest black church. (Dickerson); Chicago's second oldest Protestant church (Stanford King Institute)
claims.source: Dennis C. Dickerson, African American Preachers and Politics (secondary); Stanford King Institute (secondary)
claims.uncertainty: Low. The two phrasings ('oldest black church' / 'second oldest Protestant church') are compatible.

entities.name: Rev. Addie L. Wyatt
entities.description: Copastor of Vernon Park Church of God, Chicago; labor leader -- first female local president of the United Packinghouse Food and Allied Workers and first African-American woman elected international vice president of a major U.S. labor union (Amalgamated Meat Cutters); served on President Kennedy's Commission on the Status of Women; co-founder of the Coalition of Labor Union Women.

claims.claim: Wyatt was ordained in 1955 and served as copastor of Vernon Park Church of God in Chicago; she and her husband Claude Wyatt founded the church.
claims.evidence: Wyatt was ordained in 1955... served as copastor of Vernon Park Church of God in Chicago, Illinois.
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid for video oral history with Reverend Addie Wyatt (A2002_096)
claims.uncertainty: Low on ordination and copastor role. Church founding by the Wyatts is per a 2012 obituary (The Bluegrass Special) -- Provisional detail.

claims.claim: Wyatt was the first female local union president of the United Packinghouse Food and Allied Workers and the first African-American woman elected international vice president of a major labor union, the Amalgamated Meat Cutters.
claims.evidence: She was the first female local union president of the United Packinghouse Food and Allied Workers... became the organization's first female international vice president [of the Amalgamated Meat Cutters and Butcher Workmen of North America].
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A2002_096)
claims.uncertainty: Low; also stated in her Wikipedia biography and CTU obituary.

claims.claim: Eleanor Roosevelt appointed Wyatt to the Labor Legislation Committee of the (President Kennedy's) Commission on the Status of Women, which reported in 1963.
claims.evidence: Eleanor Roosevelt appointed her to serve on the Labor Legislation Committee of the Commission on the Status of Women, which presented its report in 1963.
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A2002_096)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Wyatt co-founded the Coalition of Labor Union Women in 1974 and delivered the keynote at its founding meeting of 3,200 participants.
claims.evidence: In 1974, she helped found the Coalition of Labor Union Women and delivered the keynote address at the founding meeting to 3,200 participants
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A2002_096)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Wyatt worked closely with Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. from 1956, helped found Operation Breadbasket, and served on the board of Operation PUSH.
claims.evidence: ordained in 1955 and the next year the Wyatts began working closely with Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. They helped found Operation Breadbasket and serve on the board of Operation PUSH
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A2002_096)
claims.uncertainty: Low-moderate. 'Helped found Operation Breadbasket' is the finding aid's phrasing; Breadbasket was launched in 1962 as SCLC's economic arm under Jesse Jackson. The Wyatt family's involvement in its early Chicago work is documented but the precise founding role is not detailed here.

claims.claim: Wyatt's papers (the Rev. Addie Wyatt and Rev. Claude Wyatt Papers) are held at the Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection, Carter G. Woodson Regional Library, Chicago.
claims.evidence: In 2010, on the South Side at the Carter G. Woodson Library, the 'Rev. Addie Wyatt and Rev. Claude Wyatt Papers,' went on display inside the library's Vivian G. Harsh Research Collection.
claims.source: Chicago Teachers Union (ctulocal1.org) obituary, 2012
claims.uncertainty: Low. This is the archival collection a future research pass should consult.

entities.name: Rev. Archibald J. Carey Jr.
entities.description: Chicago pastor (Woodlawn AME 1930-1949; Quinn Chapel AME 1949-1967), attorney, Republican alderman, federal official, and Cook County circuit judge; son of Bishop Archibald J. Carey Sr.

claims.claim: Carey pastored Woodlawn AME Church from 1930 to 1949 and Quinn Chapel AME Church from 1949 to 1967.
claims.evidence: He was pastor of Woodlawn AME Church in Chicago from 1930 to 1949 before moving to Quinn Chapel AME Church... where he served until 1967.
claims.source: The Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University (Carey, Archibald J., Jr. biography page)
claims.uncertainty: Low; corroborated by multiple secondary sources including an NIU history thesis and the Congressional Record-adjacent obituaries.

claims.claim: Carey served as Republican alderman of Chicago's Third Ward from 1947 to 1955.
claims.evidence: He served as Republican alderman of Chicago's Third Ward (1947 to 1955)... In 1955 President Dwight Eisenhower appointed Carey vice-chair and, later, chairman of the President's Committee on Government Employment Policy.
claims.source: The Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University
claims.uncertainty: Low. Also addressed the 1952 Republican National Convention in Chicago (per NIU thesis by John P. Kilstrom and encyclopedia entries).

claims.claim: Carey was an alternate member of the U.S. delegation to the Eighth General Assembly of the United Nations in 1953.
claims.evidence: was an alternate member of the United States delegation to the Eighth General Assembly of the United Nations in 1953
claims.source: The Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University
claims.uncertainty: Low. One encyclopedia entry (Alchetron) says he served as alternate delegate 1953-1956; no primary appointment document located, so duration beyond 1953 is Provisional.

claims.claim: Carey was appointed vice-chair and then chairman of the President's Committee on Government Employment Policy by President Eisenhower, becoming (per secondary sources) the first African American to chair it.
claims.evidence: In 1955 President Dwight Eisenhower appointed Carey vice-chair and, later, chairman of the President's Committee on Government Employment Policy.
claims.source: The Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University
claims.uncertainty: Low on the appointment. The 'first African American' characterization appears in encyclopedia entries (Alchetron) and a 1957 Quinn Chapel parishioners' endorsement noted in Dickerson's book; an original appointment record would strengthen it.

claims.claim: By 1966 Carey had switched parties to Democrat and was elected a Cook County circuit court judge, a position he held until his death in April 1981.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Alchetron states retirement in 1978 with one additional reappointed year -- differs from Stanford's 'at the time of his death in April 1981.'
claims.evidence: By 1966 Carey had changed his party affiliation to Democrat and was elected as a circuit court judge in Cook County, Illinois, a position he held at the time of his death in April 1981.
claims.source: The Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University
claims.uncertainty: Low. One encyclopedia entry says he served until mandatory retirement at 70 in 1978 plus one reappointed year; Stanford's account (judge at death in 1981) is preferred but the end-date detail is Provisional without a court record.

claims.claim: Carey aided the Montgomery bus boycott: King appointed him chairman of a Chicago committee on the boycott, and he helped organize an April 1956 'Hour of Prayer' that raised $2,500 for the Montgomery Improvement Association.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Historian Dennis C. Dickerson (African American Preachers and Politics: The Careys of Chicago) argues Carey's associations with J. Edgar Hoover and Mayor Daley 'compromised' his support for King -- a scholarly interpretation, not a contradiction of the boycott aid itself.
claims.evidence: King enlisted Carey's aid by appointing him chairman of a Chicago committee... During April 1956, Carey also helped organize an 'Hour of Prayer' in Chicago that raised $2,500 for the MIA.
claims.source: The Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University
claims.uncertainty: Low; sourced from the King Papers project.

entities.name: Rev. Clarence H. Cobbs
entities.description: Founder and pastor of the First Church of Deliverance (1929–1979); broadcast pioneer who built a radio/TV gospel music ministry.

claims.claim: Rev. Clarence H. Cobbs ('Preacher') was the founding pastor of the First Church of Deliverance, known for fashionable dress, informal manner, and a 200-member choir.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: 'Nicknamed "Preacher", Cobbs became known for his fashionable clothes, informal manner, and stirring performances with the church's 200-member choir. They appeared before large crowds in Comiskey Park.'
claims.source: Wikipedia (Clarence H. Cobbs)
claims.uncertainty: Secondary summary; contemporaneous press not consulted.

entities.name: Rev. Clay Evans
entities.description: Founding pastor of Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church, Chicago; founding national board chairman of Operation PUSH (1971-1976); civil rights leader, broadcaster, and gospel recording artist; ordained both Rev. Jesse Jackson and Mother Consuella York.

claims.claim: Evans was ordained a Baptist minister in 1950 and founded Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church in Chicago, which he led for roughly five decades.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Multiple secondary sources (YouTube-channel biographies, gospel press) state he founded the church in 1958, eight years after his 1950 ordination.
claims.evidence: Ordained as a Baptist Minister in 1950... Founding Pastor of the Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church of Chicago, Illinois
claims.source: Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church official site (fellowshipchicago.com, 'Meet Reverend Clay')
claims.uncertainty: Moderate on the exact founding year. The church's own site and a 2000 Senate resolution (S. Res. 395, Congressional Record) place founding in 1950; a 2019 House tribute also says 1950; gospel and press sources variously say 1958. Grade the year Disputed: 1950 (primary church source + Congressional Record) vs. 1958 (secondary press sources). Red-team harmonization (2026-09-28): founding year disputed 1950 vs 1958 across tracks.

claims.claim: Evans was the founding national board chairman of Operation PUSH (later Rainbow PUSH Coalition), serving 1971-1976, and is now its chairman emeritus.
claims.evidence: He is the Founding National Board Chairman of the Rainbow (PUSH) Coalition (Founded by Rev. Jesse L. Jackson, Sr.) holding this position for five years (1971-1976).
claims.source: Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church official site
claims.uncertainty: Low. Corroborated by the Congressional Record (Senate resolution 2000: 'founding National Board Chairman of Operation P.U.S.H. and currently serves as its Chairman Emeritus'; House tribute 2019: chairman of the board 1970-1976).

claims.claim: Evans ordained the Rev. Jesse Jackson in 1968 at Fellowship.
claims.evidence: In 1968 at his church, Rev. Evans ordained the Rev. Jesse Jackson.
claims.source: BlackFacts.com obituary summary of Rev. Evans (sourced from press obituaries)
claims.uncertainty: Low; also reported by Legacy.com's obituary and widely in press coverage of his death.
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit remediation 2026-09-28: downgraded Verified -> Provisional. Reason: Evidence field restates the claim verbatim; sole source is BlackFacts.com obituary aggregator ("sourced from press obituaries") - a cited-via chain. Source cited: BlackFacts.com obituary summary of Rev. Evans (sourced from press obituaries)

Cross-project audit remediation 2026-09-28: flagged weak_source_only (source: BlackFacts.com obituary summary of Rev. Evans (sourced from press obituaries)). Already downgraded to Provisional via regrade list; queued for re-sourcing before any public use.

claims.claim: Evans ordained Mother Consuella York, the first Black woman ordained into the Baptist clergy in Chicago (per church and community-press accounts; year reported as 1954).
claims.evidence: In 1954 Rev. Evans ordained Consuela York, known as 'Mother York,' the first Black woman to be ordained into the Baptist clergy in the city of Chicago.
claims.source: The Final Call (Dec 2019), quoting Rev. Janette Wilson of Rainbow PUSH
claims.uncertainty: Moderate. The church's own site confirms she was 'the first female to be ordained in the Baptist Denomination in Chicago' but gives no year; the 1954 date comes from a single quoted source in the Final Call. The 'first' claim is difficult to verify exhaustively against all Baptist ordinations.

claims.claim: Evans was founding president of the Broadcast Ministers' Alliance of Chicago, founding president/chair of the African American Religious Connection (1989-2006), and a board member of the National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc.
claims.evidence: He is the Founding President of the Broadcast Ministers' Alliance of Chicago (BMA), Founding President and Chairman of the African American Religious Connection (AARC) (1989 to 2006) and board member of the National Baptist Convention, U.S.A. Inc.
claims.source: Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church official site
claims.uncertainty: Low; corroborated by Congressional Record Senate resolution 2000.

claims.claim: During the Chicago Freedom Movement, Evans welcomed Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. into Fellowship despite objections and the threat of retribution from Mayor Richard J. Daley.
claims.evidence: When the Reverend Dr. Martin Luther King brought his movement to Chicago, Reverend Evans had the courage to welcome Dr. King into his church against the objections and the retribution of then-Mayor Richard J. Daley and many others.
claims.source: Congressional Record, House, Vol. 165 (2019), tribute remarks on Evans's passing
claims.uncertainty: Low on the welcome itself (also reported in press obituaries, e.g., BlackFacts/Funeral reporting citing funeral director Spencer Leak Sr. on City Hall pressure).

claims.claim: Rev. Clay Evans (1925–2019) founded Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church in 1950 and built a five-decade recording ministry with its choir; he also ordained Jesse Jackson and led Operation PUSH.
claims.evidence: PraiseIndy: founder of 'Chicago's Historic Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church... founded by Rev. Clay Evans in 1950... recorded three dozen sermon LPs and best-selling choir albums.' PragmaticObotsUnite: ordained 1950; co-founded Operation PUSH with Jesse Jackson in 1971.
claims.source: praiseindy.com (2010); pragmaticobotsunite2018.com
claims.uncertainty: Secondary summaries. Red-team harmonization (2026-09-28): founding year disputed 1950 vs 1958 across tracks.

entities.name: Rev. Dr. Jeremiah A. Wright Jr.
entities.description: Pastor emeritus of Trinity United Church of Christ, Chicago (pastor 1972-2008), which he built from 87 members to over 8,000; Black liberation theologian; Barack Obama's pastor; national figure in the 2008 presidential campaign sermon controversy.

claims.claim: Wright pastored Trinity United Church of Christ in Chicago from 1972 until his retirement in 2008, growing it from 87 members to more than 8,000.
claims.evidence: In May 2008, Wright retired as senior pastor of Trinity United Church of Christ, where he had served for 36 years. He became Pastor Emeritus. ... Wright became the pastor of Trinity Church in 1972. At the time, it was a struggling congregation with only 87 members and currently exceeds 6,000.
claims.source: BillMoyers.com guest biography
claims.uncertainty: Low on tenure. Membership figures vary (6,000 to 8,500+) across sources -- a normal range for a large congregation, not a contradiction. Red-team harmonization (2026-09-28): pastorate start disputed: 1971 (Wikipedia) vs 1972 (Alchetron/UCC tribute).

claims.claim: Wright was Barack Obama's pastor for roughly 20 years; Obama has described Wright as a spiritual mentor, and Wright's sermon inspired the title of Obama's 2006 memoir 'The Audacity of Hope.'
claims.evidence: the spotlight on a man... then-Sen. Barack Obama's minister... After 20 years, Sen. Obama cut ties with Wright. (Bill Moyers); Wright officiated at the wedding ceremony of Barack and Michelle Obama. He also baptized their children. 'The title of Obama's 2006 memoir, 'The Audacity of Hope,' was inspired by one of Wright's sermons.
claims.source: BillMoyers.com (minister relationship); Moguldom (wedding/baptism/title details)
claims.uncertainty: Low on the pastor relationship (Bill Moyers). Wedding/baptism/memoir-title details come from a single secondary source (Moguldom) -- treat those details as Provisional.
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit remediation 2026-09-28: downgraded Verified -> Provisional. Reason: Claim bundles Verified (Moyers) with Provisional parts; uncertainty itself says memoir-title details 'come from a single secondary source (Moguldom) - treat those details as Provisional.' Claim as a whole cannot be Verified. Source cited: BillMoyers.com (minister relationship); Moguldom (wedding/baptism/title details)

claims.claim: In 2007 Wright was appointed to Barack Obama's African American Religious Leadership Committee, a group of 170+ Black religious leaders backing Obama's presidential bid.
claims.evidence: In 2007, Wright was appointed to Barack Obama's African American Religious Leadership Committee, a group of more than 170 Black religious leaders who backed Obama's bid for the Democratic nomination.
claims.source: Moguldom, '15 Things To Know About Obama's Ex-Pastor, Rev. Jeremiah Wright'
claims.uncertainty: Moderate; single secondary source, not independently corroborated in this pass.

claims.claim: Wright served on multiple institutional boards, including the Board of Trustees of Virginia Union University, Chicago Theological Seminary, and the City Colleges of Chicago, plus Evangelical Health Systems, the Black Theology Project, the Center for New Horizons, and Malcolm X College's School of Nursing.
claims.evidence: He served on the Board of Trustees of Virginia Union University, the Chicago Theological Seminary, and the City Colleges of Chicago. Wright was also a board member of other religious, civic, and educational organizations, such as Evangelical Health Systems, Black Theology Project, Center for New Horizons, and Malcolm X School of Nursing at Malcolm X College in Chicago.
claims.source: BlackFacts.com (Jeremiah A. Wright profile, citing BlackPast)
claims.uncertainty: Moderate. Single secondary source listing boards; an institutional bio or board minutes would be needed to confirm each. This is the fullest public record found of his civic-institutional footprint, which was board/service-based rather than officeholding.

claims.claim: In spring 2008, excerpts of Wright's sermons became a national controversy in the presidential campaign; Obama denounced the sermons and distanced himself from Wright.
claims.evidence: In the spring of 2008, Rev. Dr. Jeremiah Wright... became embroiled in controversy for 'inflammatory rhetoric'... After 20 years, Sen. Obama cut ties with Wright.
claims.source: BillMoyers.com guest biography
claims.uncertainty: Low; extensively documented in 2008 press.

entities.name: Rev. Dr. Willie T. Barrow
entities.description: Ordained minister and Chicago civil rights leader ('The Little Warrior'); SCLC field organizer; co-founder of Operation Breadbasket; first woman executive director/CEO of Operation PUSH and later chairman/CEO of the Rainbow PUSH Coalition.

claims.claim: Barrow was ordained as a minister after attending Warner-Pacific Theological Seminary in Portland, Oregon; she came to Chicago in 1945 and worked as a youth minister.
claims.evidence: Barrow later attended Warner-Pacific Theological Seminary in Portland, Oregon... Upon graduation, Barrow was ordained as a minister and began her career as both a spiritual and social activist. (HistoryMakers); In 1945, she came to Chicago and worked as a youth minister (Congressional Record, 2015).
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A1999_001); Congressional Record, Senate, Vol. 161 (2015), tribute remarks
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Barrow was a field organizer for Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. and the SCLC (1953-1965), organizing transportation, shelter, meetings and rallies for demonstrations including the 1965 Selma march; she also helped organize the 1963 March on Washington.
claims.evidence: From 1953 to 1965, she was a field organizer for Reverend Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. and the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, where she was responsible for the organization of transportation, shelter, meetings and rallies for demonstrations, including the 1965 March on Selma, Alabama. (HistoryMakers); she also helped organize the 1963 march on Washington. (Congressional Record)
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A1999_001); Congressional Record, Senate, Vol. 161 (2015)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Barrow was a founding member of Operation Breadbasket in Chicago (founded with Rev. Jesse Jackson), which became the Rainbow PUSH Coalition.
claims.evidence: During the 1960s, Barrow was among the founding members of Operation Breadbasket in Chicago, Illinois (HistoryMakers); She, with Rev. Jackson, was a co-founder of Operation Breadbasket, which became the Rainbow-PUSH Coalition. (NPR Illinois, 2015)
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A1999_001); NPR Illinois obituary
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Barrow became executive director of Operation PUSH in 1984 -- the first woman to lead a major civil rights organization -- and later served as chairman of the board and CEO of the Rainbow PUSH Coalition.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None located on the PUSH roles themselves.
claims.evidence: Barrow replaced Jackson as executive director of Operation PUSH in 1984 (Citizen Newspaper Group, 2015); In 1984, Barrow became the first woman executive director of a civil rights organization, serving as Push's CEO. (Wikipedia); as Operation Breadbasket evolved into the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition, Reverend Barrow became the first woman to lead the organization. As the chairman of the board and CEO... (Congressional Record, 2015)
claims.source: Citizen Newspaper Group; Wikipedia; Congressional Record, Senate, Vol. 161 (2015)
claims.uncertainty: Low on the roles and 1984 date; the 'first woman to lead a civil rights organization' framing is press characterization (Coretta Scott King led the King Center, founded 1968, so the claim's scope should be read narrowly).

claims.claim: Barrow was a mentor to Black political leaders including Rev. Jesse Jackson and Barack Obama, and advocated for the elections of Harold Washington and Barack Obama.
claims.evidence: Rev. Willie T. Barrow, a long-time Chicago activist and mentor to black political leaders -- including Rev. Jesse Jackson and President Barack Obama (NPR Illinois); she pushed for the election of the city's first African-American mayor, Harold Washington, and the nation's first African-American president, Barack Obama. (Citizen Newspaper Group); Around Chicago, she was known as 'godmother' for the work she did with many young community activists -- including Barack Obama. (Congressional Record, 2015)
claims.source: NPR Illinois; Citizen Newspaper Group; Congressional Record, Senate, Vol. 161 (2015)
claims.uncertainty: Low on mentorship and electoral advocacy; these are documented campaign-support roles, not staff positions. The 'godmother of President Barack Obama' phrasing (Wikipedia) is informal, not a legal or familial relationship.

entities.name: Rev. Jesse L. Jackson Sr.
entities.description: Baptist minister ordained in 1968 at Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church, Chicago; appointed by King to lead Chicago Operation Breadbasket (1966); founder of Operation PUSH (1971) and the National Rainbow Coalition; two-time candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination (1984, 1988); Chicago-based national civil rights leader.

claims.claim: Jackson was chosen by Dr. King in 1966 to head the Chicago branch of Operation Breadbasket and became its national director in 1967.
claims.evidence: 1966 - Is chosen by King to head the Chicago branch of Operation Breadbasket... A year later he is appointed national director.
claims.source: CNN Fast Facts: Jesse Jackson
claims.uncertainty: Low; corroborated by Religion News Service obituary and Chicago History Museum (Google Arts & Culture).

claims.claim: Jackson was ordained a Baptist minister in 1968 (at Fellowship Missionary Baptist Church, Chicago, by Rev. Clay Evans).
claims.evidence: 1968 - Is ordained a Baptist minister. (CNN); In 1968 at his church, Rev. Evans ordained the Rev. Jesse Jackson. (BlackFacts/Legacy)
claims.source: CNN Fast Facts; BlackFacts.com obituary summary
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: In December 1971 Jackson resigned from the SCLC and founded Operation PUSH (People United to Save/S... Serve Humanity) in Chicago, serving as executive director 1971-1986.
claims.evidence: December 1971 - Resigns from the SCLC and forms Operation PUSH (People United to Save Humanity) in Chicago. 1971-1986 - Executive director of operation for PUSH.
claims.source: CNN Fast Facts: Jesse Jackson
claims.uncertainty: Low. The organization's name was later changed to 'People United to Serve Humanity' (per multiple sources).

claims.claim: Jackson ran for the Democratic presidential nomination in 1984 and 1988, and founded the National Rainbow Coalition in the mid-1980s (sources date it 1984-1986).
claims.contradictory_evidence: RNS (2026-02-17) dates the National Rainbow Coalition founding to 1984; Citizen Newspaper Group (2015) to 1985.
claims.evidence: November 3, 1983 - Formally announces his candidacy for the 1984 Democratic presidential nomination... October 10, 1987 - Formally announces his candidacy for the 1988 Presidential election. April 17, 1986 - Founds the National Rainbow Coalition
claims.source: CNN Fast Facts: Jesse Jackson
claims.uncertainty: Low on the campaigns. The Rainbow Coalition founding year is Disputed across sources: CNN says April 17, 1986; RNS obituary says 1984; Citizen Newspaper Group says 1985. The 1986 date is the most specific (day-month) but the discrepancy is noted.

claims.claim: Jackson died in February 2026 at age 84.
claims.evidence: 'I am somebody!': Jesse Jackson, civil rights leader who ran for presidency, dies at 84
claims.source: Religion News Service obituary
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Rev. Joseph H. Jackson
entities.description: Pastor of Olivet Baptist Church, Chicago, 1941-1990; president of the National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc. 1953-1982; leading Black clerical voice against direct-action civil rights tactics.

claims.claim: Jackson pastored Olivet Baptist Church in Chicago from 1941 until his death in 1990.
claims.evidence: moving to Chicago in 1941, to serve as pastor of Olivet Baptist Church, a position he held until his death in 1990
claims.source: The Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University (Jackson, Joseph Harrison biography page)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

claims.claim: Jackson was elected president of the National Baptist Convention in 1953 and headed it for roughly three decades (through 1982).
claims.evidence: In 1953, Jackson was elected president of the NBC, which he headed for the next three decades.
claims.source: The Martin Luther King, Jr. Research and Education Institute, Stanford University
claims.uncertainty: Low. BlackPast.org dates the presidency 1953-1982 and encyclopedia entries say 29 years; the end year 1982 is corroborated by multiple sources.

claims.claim: Jackson was the leading public spokesperson for Black conservative opposition to the direct-action civil rights movement, arguing in a widely reported 1964 address that the vote, not civil disobedience, was the effective weapon for civil rights.
claims.evidence: Rev. Joseph Jackson, long time pastor of Olivet Baptist Church in Chicago, Illinois, and President of the National Baptist Convention from 1953 to 1982 became the leading spokesperson for the black conservative opposition to the direct action civil rights movement... [address at the NBC's 84th annual meeting held in Detroit, on September 19, 1964]
claims.source: BlackPast.org (reprint of the 1964 address text)
claims.uncertainty: Low; the address text is reproduced in full. Characterization as 'leading spokesperson' is the secondary source's editorial framing.

claims.claim: Jackson did not support nonviolent direct action and did not support the Chicago Freedom Movement.
claims.evidence: He did not support nonviolent direct action. He did not support the Chicago Freedom Movement.
claims.source: Chicago Freedom Movement digital archive, Middlebury College (biographical note)
claims.uncertainty: Low; consistent with his published 1964 address and the King Papers record of his clashes with King.

claims.claim: Jackson was the only Baptist observer invited by Pope John XXIII to the Second Vatican Council (1962), after meeting the Pope a year earlier.
claims.evidence: Whereas the World Baptist Alliance declined to pursue an invitation to Vatican II, Jackson was the only Baptist observer invited by Pope John XXIII. Jackson had met the Pope a year prior... (citing New York Times, 10-18-62)
claims.source: Patheos/Anxious Bench blog (guest contributor), citing the New York Times, October 18, 1962
claims.uncertainty: Moderate. The 'only Baptist observer' claim rests on a single blog post citing a 1962 NYT article; the underlying NYT article was not retrieved in this pass.

claims.claim: When the Chicago City Council renamed South Parkway (where Olivet stood) for Martin Luther King Jr. after King's assassination, Jackson altered the church's main entrance and address to avoid association with King's name.
claims.evidence: when Chicago city council, months after King's assassination, decided to change the name of South Parkway... to Martin Luther King Boulevard, Jackson reacted to the prospect by altering the main entrance and address of the church so as to avoid any association with King's name.
claims.source: European Journal of American Studies, 'Missions of Patriotism: Joseph H. Jackson and Martin Luther King' (peer-reviewed article)
claims.uncertainty: Moderate. Single peer-reviewed source citing secondary material (Abernathy memoir); no corroborating press account located in this pass.

entities.name: Roberta Martin
entities.description: Gospel composer, pianist, and choral organizer; founder of the Roberta Martin Singers; developed the gospel piano accompaniment style.

claims.claim: Roberta Martin (1907–1969) began as pianist for Ebenezer's Young People's Choir and in 1933 organized the Martin-Frye Quartet (later the Roberta Martin Singers) with Dorsey's and Frye's help.
claims.evidence: Smithsonian NMAH AC-0408: 'In 1933, with the help of Dorsey and Frye, Roberta Martin organized the Martin Frye Quartet with Eugene Smith, James Lawrence, Robert Anderson, Willie Webb, and Norsalus McKissick. This group became the Roberta Martin Singers in 1936.'
claims.source: Smithsonian NMAH Archives AC-0408 (Bernice Johnson Reagon program notes, 1981)
claims.uncertainty: Archival program notes prepared 1981; consistent with other biographies.

claims.claim: Martin incorporated the Roberta Martin Studio of Music (publishing house) in 1939 and launched James Cleveland's career as composer/arranger after he sang in the Gospelaires.
claims.evidence: FromTheVaults biography: publishing house incorporated 1939; published works by Alex Bradford and James Cleveland. Wikipedia: 'After the trio disbanded, an associate of the group, Roberta Martin, hired [James Cleveland] as a composer and arranger.'
claims.source: fromthevaults-boppinbob.blogspot.com; Wikipedia
claims.uncertainty: Secondary sources; incorporation records not retrieved.

entities.name: Roberta Martin Singers
entities.description: Premier Chicago gospel ensemble (1933–1970) grown from Ebenezer Baptist's junior choir; recorded for Fidelity, Apollo, and Savoy; training ground for major gospel artists.

claims.claim: The Roberta Martin Singers (1933–1970), founded as the Martin-Frye Quartet at Ebenezer Baptist, recorded first for Fidelity Records in 1947, then Religious Records and Apollo (1949–1955), and later Savoy.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia: first recording for Fidelity Records in 1947 as 'Roberta Martin Singers of Chicago' ('Precious Memories'); then Religious Records of Detroit through 1947, Apollo 1949–1955; labels listed as Fidelity, Apollo, Savoy. HistoryMakers: under Savoy contract by 1957; 1958 hit 'God Specializes.'
claims.source: Wikipedia; The HistoryMakers oral history finding aid (2012 interview)
claims.uncertainty: Recording chronology is from secondary compilations; session-level discography not verified here.

claims.claim: The group pioneered a mixed-voice gospel ensemble sound and launched careers including James Cleveland, Delois Barrett Campbell, and the Barrett Sisters.
claims.evidence: Chicago landmark report (Morning Star Baptist): DeLois Barrett Campbell was recruited by the Roberta Martin Singers as a high school student; Delois and sisters formed the Barrett Sisters in 1950. Wikipedia: James Cleveland was hired as composer/arranger.
claims.source: City of Chicago Landmark Designation Report, Morning Star Baptist (chicago.gov); Wikipedia
claims.uncertainty: Landmark report is a primary municipal designation document citing Ebony (1988).
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit 2026-09-28: source_type primary -> secondary. Source mixes an institutional/finding-aid reference with Wikipedia or weak components; "primary" is reserved for primary records directly consulted and establishing the fact. Source: City of Chicago Landmark Designation Report, Morning Star Baptist (chicago.gov); Wikipedia

entities.name: Sallie Martin
entities.description: Gospel singer, arranger, and businesswoman called the 'Mother of Gospel Music'; co-founded the NCGCC with Dorsey and later Martin & Morris Publishing.

claims.claim: Sallie Martin (1895–1988) moved to Chicago in 1929, joined a chorus directed by Dorsey, and co-founded the NCGCC with him in 1933.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on her role; the 1932 vs. 1933 NCGCC date dispute noted above applies.
claims.evidence: BlackPast: Martin moved to Chicago by 1929, joined a Dorsey-directed chorus, and co-founded the NCGCC with him in 1933. She served as Dorsey's song demonstrator and bookkeeper through the 1930s, singing and selling his compositions at churches and conventions.
claims.source: BlackPast.org (Janet Hauck)
claims.uncertainty: BlackPast is a reference encyclopedia; its underlying archival citations were not retrieved.

claims.claim: In 1940 Martin left Dorsey and co-founded Martin and Morris Publishing with Kenneth Morris; the Sallie Martin Singers became one of the first all-female gospel groups and recorded for Capitol in 1949.
claims.evidence: BlackPast: 'In 1940, she left Dorsey to help start the Martin and Morris Publishing Company, which published the famous Just a Closer Walk with Thee.' KWBU/Baylor Black Gospel Music Preservation Program: her Capitol 1949 recording of '(Jesus is the Answer) He's All I Need.' Ravishly notes her group trained future stars including Brother Joe May and Dinah Washington.
claims.source: BlackPast.org; KWBU 'SHOUT! Black Gospel Music Moments' (2022); Ravishly (2015)
claims.uncertainty: Specific month/day of the 1940 split not established in these sources.

entities.name: St. Mark United Methodist Church
entities.description: United Methodist congregation at 8441 S. St. Lawrence Ave., Chicago (Chatham/far South Side). Founded 1893 as St. Mark Methodist Episcopal Church in a Bronzeville storefront; described by the church as the largest African-American church in the United Methodist Northern Illinois Conference; 125th-anniversary history published 2019.

claims.claim: Founded 1893 on Chicago's South Side as St. Mark Methodist Episcopal Church, initially in a storefront on State Street in Bronzeville; Rev. S.C. Goosley was invited to Chicago to develop a Methodist presence in the African-American community.
claims.evidence: The church's own website states founding in 1893; the 125th-anniversary book summary (Parker, Arcadia 2019) gives the storefront origin and Rev. S.C. Goosley's invitation.
claims.source: stmarkumcchicago.org; Daniel T. Parker, 'St. Mark United Methodist Church' (Arcadia Publishing, 2019) — synopsis.
claims.uncertainty: The 1893 founding is consistent across the church's own site and the anniversary book compiled from church archives.
claims.contradictory_evidence: A low-quality directory site (churcheslist.com) lists an implausible '1784' founding; disregarded as unreliable.

claims.claim: In 1907 the church moved to 50th Street and Wabash Avenue, worshipping there until 1959, when it moved to its present far-South-Side location at 8441 S. St. Lawrence Ave.
claims.evidence: Parker anniversary-book summary; church site confirms current address.
claims.source: Daniel T. Parker, 'St. Mark United Methodist Church' (Arcadia, 2019) — synopsis; stmarkumcchicago.org.
claims.uncertainty: Sourced to the book's promotional synopsis, not the book's full text; exact 1959 move details and the circumstances (neighborhood change) await the primary text or Defender coverage.

claims.claim: The largest African-American church in the United Methodist Northern Illinois Conference.
claims.evidence: Church's own website and affiliated listings state this.
claims.source: stmarkumcchicago.org; foreverywoman.org service listing (quoting church).
claims.uncertainty: Congregation's own claim; conference-level membership data not consulted.

claims.claim: A 125th-anniversary illustrated history by lifetime member Daniel T. Parker was published by Arcadia Publishing in 2019, compiled from the church's archives and longtime congregants' contributions.
claims.evidence: Publisher listings (Tertulia, AbeBooks, Past Forward) with full bibliographic details and author bio.
claims.source: Arcadia Publishing listing via tertulia.com/abebooks.com (ISBN 9781467103282), 2019.
claims.uncertainty: None on the book's existence and provenance claim; the book's full text was not consulted.

entities.name: Storefront Church Phenomenon (Black Chicago)
entities.description: The dominant form of Black religious organization in migration-era Chicago: small congregations meeting in rented commercial spaces, led by minimally credentialed clergy, serving Southern migrants alienated from old-line churches.

claims.claim: A 1930 survey found storefronts comprised 72% of African American churches in Chicago (vs. 54% Baltimore, 48% Philadelphia, 45% Detroit).
claims.contradictory_evidence: No contradictory figure found, but the survey's sampling method is not described in the secondary reporting; Noreen's later (1965) work is a name-list, not a census, so the 72% has not been independently re-verified.
claims.evidence: Reported in Boyd (1998), The Social Science Journal 35(3), citing Mays & Nicholson, The Negro's Church (1933), p. 219. Corroborated in public-history summary by Rogers Park/West Ridge Historical Society (citing Boyd).
claims.source: Benjamin E. Mays & Joseph W. Nicholson, The Negro's Church (1933), via Robert L. Boyd (1998)
claims.uncertainty: Survey methodology (how 'storefront' was defined, sampling frame, South-side vs. citywide coverage) is unknown from the secondary report; treat the 72% as a Provisional estimate from an early-20th-century survey, not a census.

claims.claim: Black storefront churches concentrated in three denominations: Baptist, Holiness, and Spiritualist.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Noreen's 1965 Chicago name-list adds nuance: 8% Church of God in Christ and 4% Pentecostal/Spiritualist appear as named denominations, with 69% Baptist -- broadly consistent, but COGIC (Pentecostal) is separately enumerated there.
claims.evidence: Mays & Nicholson (1933, p. 313) via Boyd (1998); consistent with Allan Spear's Black Chicago (1967) account of growth in small Holiness and Pentecostal groups, and Noreen (1965) denominational breakdown of 381 Chicago storefront church names.
claims.source: Mays & Nicholson (1933) via Boyd (1998); Noreen, Names 13(1) (1965); Spear (1967)
claims.uncertainty: Denominational self-identification in storefront names is loose; Noreen notes denominational ties 'may be very weak.'

claims.claim: Storefront congregations typically rented quarters originally designed for small businesses, seldom owning buildings or grounds, often clustered several to a block along commercial corridors.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; this is consistently described across observers.
claims.evidence: Noreen (1965): 'Most of them occupy quarters originally designed for small businesses. Seldom do these churches have buildings and grounds in addition to the main storefront... on Roosevelt Road I have seen four adjacent churches.' Stronks (1962-64) lists churches along West Roosevelt Road. Jordano (2009) documents sanctuaries in 'repurposed commercial spaces.'
claims.source: Noreen (1965); Stronks (1962-64); Jordano (2009)
claims.uncertainty: Observational; some storefronts were in houses rather than commercial buildings (Noreen notes 'a few can be found in houses').

claims.claim: The storefront ministry was an 'ethnic niche': easy to enter (no certification or formal education required), meeting migrants' unmet demand for traditional, demonstrative, intimate worship that old-line churches did not supply; it provided social and psychological support to migrants.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Wallace Best (2007) does not contradict the niche framing but reorients its valence: storefront/Pentecostal churches were not merely compensatory or otherworldly but religiously innovative and community-active.
claims.evidence: Boyd (1998): storefront ministers attracted migrants away from established churches whose 'dicty' members snubbed newcomers; old-line pastors denounced them as 'jack-leg preachers' yet imitated them to 'hold the masses' (Drake & Cayton 1962, p. 631). Grossman (1989) quoted: migrants formed churches 'frequently joining with former townsmen or other dissatisfied migrants.' Boyd concludes the storefront church was 'an important institution in the African American community' offering social support.
claims.source: Robert L. Boyd, The Social Science Journal 35(3) (1998)
claims.uncertainty: Analytical framework (ethnic niche theory) applied to historical data; the 'easy entry' claim rests partly on a 1934 national survey (Woodson: 83% of Black ministers had no theological training). Chicago-specific entry-barrier data not isolated.

entities.name: The Woodlawn Organization (TWO)
entities.description: South Side community organization founded in 1959 out of the cooperative efforts of clergymen in the Greater Woodlawn Pastors' Alliance; influenced by Saul Alinsky's organizing model; confronted slum landlords, the University of Chicago's urban renewal program, and inadequate schools.

claims.claim: The Woodlawn Organization grew out of the Greater Woodlawn Pastors' Alliance in 1959 and used Alinsky-style confrontation tactics against unfair business practices, slum landlords, University of Chicago urban renewal, and inadequate school facilities.
claims.evidence: ERIC ED035799, 'Black Self-Determination: The Story of the Woodlawn Organization' (1969, Eerdmans): 'grew out of cooperative efforts of clergymen in the area, members of the Greater Woodlawn Pastor's Alliance, in 1959... influenced by the thinking of Saul Alinsky... directly to confront unfair business practices, slum landlords, the University of Chicago's urban renewal program, inadequate school facilities.'
claims.uncertainty: Summary record of a 1969 publication; TWO's papers and Alinsky's Industrial Areas Foundation records would be primary.

claims.claim: Bishop Arthur Brazier was a founder and spokesman of The Woodlawn Organization, organized with Alinsky's IAF, and led its 1963 fight against University of Chicago expansion.
claims.evidence: Brazier became the spokesman for the Temporary Woodlawn Organization (TWO), organized by Nicholas Von Hoffman of Saul Alinsky's Industrial Areas Foundation. Brazier successfully led TWO against the expansion of the University of Chicago in 1963. (HistoryMakers)
claims.source: The HistoryMakers, finding aid (A2005_003) (primary)
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Theodore Frye
entities.description: Gospel singer and choir director; Dorsey's collaborator at Ebenezer Baptist Church; first public performer of 'Precious Lord.'

claims.claim: Theodore Frye directed the junior choir at Ebenezer Baptist Church with Thomas A. Dorsey and performed the first public singing of 'Take My Hand, Precious Lord' at Ebenezer in 1932.
claims.contradictory_evidence: A Logos sermon source (citing WSJ) says Dorsey 'debuted' Precious Lord for the Pilgrim congregation — in tension with the Ebenezer-first accounts. This may reflect Dorsey's dual 1932 appointments rather than two separate debuts.
claims.evidence: Smithsonian Archives (NMAH AC-0408, Bernice Johnson Reagon program notes): Dorsey and Frye directed the Young People's Choir of Ebenezer Baptist Church. Southeastsun: Frye's choir sang 'Precious Lord' the Sunday after Dorsey played it for Frye. MDPI peer-reviewed article: 'Dorsey and then-musical collaborator Theodore Frye introduced Precious Lord to the congregation at Ebenezer Baptist Church less than a month after Nettie's death... (Harris 1994, p. 241).'
claims.source: Smithsonian NMAH Archives AC-0408; MDPI Religions 10(4), 285 (2019) citing Michael Harris, 1994
claims.uncertainty: The Smithsonian program notes are primary archival material from a 1981 concert series; the 1932 events are recalled secondhand through Dorsey's oral history as transmitted by Harris (1994).

claims.claim: Roberta Martin served as pianist/accompanist for the Ebenezer junior choir directed by Dorsey and Frye.
claims.evidence: Smithsonian NMAH AC-0408: 'Martin's first church position was as a pianist for the Young Peoples' Choir of Ebenezer Baptist Church in Chicago. There she worked with Thomas A. Dorsey and Theodore Frye.' Wikipedia/Ebenezer accounts concur.
claims.source: Smithsonian NMAH Archives AC-0408; Wikipedia
claims.uncertainty: Archival notes; consistent across sources.
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit 2026-09-28: source_type primary -> secondary. Source mixes an institutional/finding-aid reference with Wikipedia or weak components; "primary" is reserved for primary records directly consulted and establishing the fact. Source: Smithsonian NMAH Archives AC-0408; Wikipedia

entities.name: Thomas A. Dorsey
entities.description: Chicago-based composer and pianist known as the 'Father of Gospel Music'; served as music director of Pilgrim Baptist Church from 1932 to the late 1970s; founded the first Black-owned gospel publishing house.

claims.claim: Thomas A. Dorsey (1899–1993) became choir/choral director of Pilgrim Baptist Church in 1932, serving until the late 1970s.
claims.evidence: Multiple outlets state Dorsey became choral director at Pilgrim Baptist in 1932 and held the post until the late 1970s. The NMAAHC confirms he was hired in the 1930s as music director by Pastor Junius C. Austin and that the church became known as the birthplace of gospel music under his tenure.
claims.source: GRAMMY.com/National Museum of Gospel Music reporting; National Trust for Historic Preservation, Preservation magazine; NMAAHC object record nmaahc_2015.134.1a-g
claims.uncertainty: Only the year (1932) and the long tenure are consistent across sources; the NMAAHC object record says 'in the 1930s' rather than naming 1932.
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit harmonization 2026-09-28. H1: this 1932 claim confirmed as the corpus position; BVM-005's 1931 claims corrected to match.

claims.claim: Dorsey turned to gospel composition after his wife Nettie and infant son died in August 1932; he composed 'Take My Hand, Precious Lord' in their wake.
claims.contradictory_evidence: MDPI article shows death certificate dated September 30, 1932, vs. the August 1932 date in popular biographies.
claims.evidence: Biographical accounts report Nettie Dorsey died in childbirth while Dorsey was in St. Louis (August 1932); his son died two days later; he then wrote 'Precious Lord.' A peer-reviewed MDPI article reproduces Nettie Dorsey's death certificate (30 September 1932 — note discrepancy) and cites Dorsey's own recollection via Harris (1994).
claims.source: GRAMMY.com; LA Sentinel; MDPI Religions 10(4), 285 (2019)
claims.uncertainty: Secondary retellings compress and sometimes dramatize events; the death certificate image in the MDPI article is dated 30 Sept 1932, conflicting with the August 1932 timeline given in popular accounts.

claims.claim: Dorsey established Dorsey House of Music in 1932, the first Black-owned gospel music publishing house in the U.S., selling his sheet music through churches.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None on 1932 or the 'first Black-owned gospel publishing house' claim; minor variation in who co-founded it.
claims.evidence: LA Sentinel: 'In 1932, he established Dorsey House of Music, the first Black gospel music publishing company.' Wikipedia's Dorsey article: Dorsey and Sallie Martin 'established a publishing company called Dorsey House of Music, the first black-owned gospel publishing house in the U.S.'
claims.source: LA Sentinel (Feb 7, 2018); Wikipedia citing Heilbut and other scholarship
claims.uncertainty: The co-founding role of Sallie Martin vs. Dorsey alone is not fully disambiguated in sources.

entities.name: Trinity United Church of Christ
entities.description: United Church of Christ congregation at 400 W. 95th St., Chicago (Roseland/far South Side). Founded December 3, 1961 by twelve middle-class Black families; led by Rev. Dr. Jeremiah A. Wright Jr. from the early 1970s to 2008, growing into the largest congregation in the UCC denomination; church of Barack and Michelle Obama.

claims.claim: On December 3, 1961, twelve middle-class Black families — most descendants of Great Migration migrants — met for worship in a Chicago elementary school gymnasium, founding Trinity; the first pastor was Rev. Kenneth B. Smith (1961-1966).
claims.evidence: Encyclopedic accounts (Wikipedia, Citizendium) and the church's own site all give the December 3, 1961 date, the twelve families, the school-gymnasium setting, and Smith as first pastor.
claims.source: Wikipedia 'Trinity United Church of Christ'; tucc.org (church's own site); Citizendium.
claims.uncertainty: Consistent across independent sources; no conflicting founding date found.

claims.claim: Rev. Dr. Jeremiah A. Wright Jr. became pastor on March 1 (1971 or 1972); the congregation had about 250 members on the rolls with roughly 90 attending; by 2008 Trinity had grown to more than 8,000 members and 70 ministries.
claims.evidence: Wikipedia's Jeremiah Wright article gives March 1, 1971, ~250 members/~90 attending; Alchetron's Wright biography gives March 1, 1972; a 2008-era profile gives 8,000+ members and 70 ministries; UCC President John H. Thomas's 2008 statement thanks Wright for 36 years of leadership.
claims.source: Wikipedia 'Jeremiah Wright'; Alchetron 'Jeremiah Wright'; In These Times profile (2005); UCC President's statement (2008).
claims.uncertainty: Sources conflict on whether Wright began March 1, 1971 or March 1, 1972 (a 36-year tenure ending in early 2008 points to 1972). The membership growth figures are broadly consistent across sources.

claims.claim: By March 2008 Trinity was the largest congregation in the (predominantly white) United Church of Christ denomination.
claims.evidence: Statement by UCC President and General Minister John H. Thomas; reported in encyclopedic coverage.
claims.source: UCC President John H. Thomas statement (March 2008), via Wikipedia 'Jeremiah Wright.'
claims.uncertainty: Denominational-leadership statement; denomination membership statistics not independently consulted.
red_team_notes: Cross-project audit remediation 2026-09-28: downgraded Verified -> Provisional and flagged weak_source_only. Source rests solely on weak/laundered sources (UCC President John H. Thomas statement (March 2008), via Wikipedia 'Jeremiah Wright.'); queued for re-sourcing before any public use.

claims.claim: Barack Obama joined Trinity in the late 1980s, was baptized there, and he and Michelle Obama were married at Trinity on October 3, 1992, by Rev. Wright; Obama credited Wright's 'The Audacity of Hope' sermon with introducing him to Jesus Christ.
claims.evidence: Widely reported contemporaneous coverage; Obama's own testimony (quoted in GetReligion and campaign-era profiles) describes attending Trinity on 95th Street and hearing Wright's sermon.
claims.source: GetReligion/Obama testimony; In These Times profile (2005); answers.com compiled references.
claims.uncertainty: Public historical fact, multiply attested; no doctrinal claims made here.

claims.claim: Current campus at 400 W. 95th St., Chicago; the present building dates to approximately 1997 (Brook Architecture describes a '20-year-old building' in its 2017 renovation project); a $5 million 'Raise the Roof' campaign (2017) added a green roof, rain gardens, and infrastructure upgrades.
claims.evidence: Church's own site (tucc.org), FaithStreet listing, and Brook Architecture project page.
claims.source: tucc.org; brookarchitecture.com Trinity project page (2017).
claims.uncertainty: The ~1997 building date is inferred from the '20-year-old building' phrasing in 2017; the date the congregation moved to 95th Street was not established.

claims.claim: Trinity UCC owns and operates Imani Village, a social enterprise community development in Pullman's 95th Street corridor, planned as an eco-friendly intergenerational mixed-use development with affordable housing, urban farm, and services.
claims.contradictory_evidence: Acreage discrepancy: 27 vs. 32 acres across sources.
claims.evidence: WLOV/Next City (June 2024): 'Imani Village is a social enterprise owned and operated by the nearby Trinity United Church of Christ.' Christian Century (Oct 10, 2017): 27-acre project with five-acre farm for green-jobs training for returning citizens, senior housing, youth athletics, and a primary-care clinic via hospital partnership.
claims.source: 995wlov.com (June 28, 2024); Christian Century, October 10, 2017
claims.uncertainty: Acreage varies by source (27 acres in Christian Century; 32 acres in WLOV/Next City). Development is phased and ongoing.

claims.claim: Imani Village's senior residence at 9621 S. Cottage Grove Ave. (70 units: 60 one-bedroom, 10 two-bedroom; rents $214-$1,140) received $13.9 million in city Department of Housing financing and was ribbon-cut in November 2025 with Mayor Brandon Johnson and Rev. Dr. Otis Moss III.
claims.evidence: City of Chicago press release (chicago.gov): financing details, unit mix, AMI targeting (8 units at 15% AMI, 8 at 30%, 54 at 60%), and Moss quote.
claims.source: City of Chicago press release, 'Mayor Brandon Johnson Cuts Ribbon On Imani Village Senior Residence,' November 2025 (chicago.gov)
claims.uncertainty: None material; government press release with specifics.

claims.claim: Imani Village's clinic (in partnership with Advocate Health), childcare center, and community space are already open and in use.
claims.evidence: WLOV/Next City (June 2024): 'Imani Village's clinic is already open as is a childcare center and a community space that's already been used for events like baby showers.'
claims.source: 995wlov.com (June 28, 2024)
claims.uncertainty: Single journalistic source; program details (capacity, services) not independently confirmed.

claims.claim: Under Wright (1972-2008), Trinity grew from 87 members to over 8,000 and became one of the most politically active and socially conscious churches in the nation.
claims.evidence: Wright became the pastor of Trinity Church in 1972. At the time, it was a struggling congregation with only 87 members... Rev. Wright's efforts to address the needs of the community had made Trinity one of the most politically active and socially conscious churches in the nation. (Bill Moyers)
claims.source: BillMoyers.com (secondary); Los Angeles Sentinel (secondary)
claims.uncertainty: Low. Red-team harmonization (2026-09-28): pastorate start disputed: 1971 (Wikipedia) vs 1972 (Alchetron/UCC tribute).

entities.name: Usher Boards
entities.description: Lay ministry of doorkeepers ('watchmen and watchwomen') managing welcome, order, offerings, and care during worship; honored with an annual Usher's Day.

claims.claim: Usher boards serve as the sanctuary's infrastructure of order and welcome: ushers arrive about an hour before service, prepare programs and offering envelopes, seat latecomers, stand watch throughout the service, use as many as 23 silent hand signals, care for worshippers overcome during spirit possession, handle offerings, and are among the last to leave.
claims.contradictory_evidence: None found; described as consistent across Black church traditions.
claims.evidence: African American Lectionary cultural resources: Eli Wilson Jr., 'Ushers as the Infrastructure for Process and Order' (2008); Tammy L. Kernodle, Ushers Day cultural resources (2010): ushers are 'the initial source of love and welcome,' trained in hand signals and (via the Nurses Guild auxiliary) CPR/first aid; Usher's Day is an annual congregational observance honoring the board.
claims.source: The African American Lectionary (theafricanamericanlectionary.org), cultural resource commentaries
claims.uncertainty: Descriptive liturgical resource rather than ethnographic study; the 23-hand-signal figure is reported as what 'many' ushers are taught, not a universal count.

entities.name: Vernon Park Church of God
entities.description: Church pastored by Rev. Claude Wyatt during the 1982-83 voter registration drive; operated a mobile voter-registration van outside the church on Sunday mornings.

claims.claim: Pastor Claude Wyatt parked a mobile registration van outside Vernon Park Church of God on Sunday mornings during the 1982-83 registration drive, and Washington asked Wyatt to join the campaign's steering committee.
claims.evidence: Christianity Today (May 1983): 'Wyatt himself had a mobile registration van parked outside his church on Sunday mornings... Washington asked Wyatt and Harry Gibson, pastor of the Saint Mark United Methodist Church, to join the campaign's steering committee.'
claims.source: Christianity Today, 'Why Black Brethren Embrace Politics,' May 1983
claims.uncertainty: Single contemporary source.

claims.claim: Addie Wyatt served as copastor of Vernon Park Church of God; she and her husband Claude Wyatt founded the church.
claims.evidence: Wyatt also served as copastor of Vernon Park Church of God in Chicago, Illinois. (HistoryMakers); At the Vernon Park Church of God on Chicago's South Side, founded by Rev. Wyatt and her husband Claude Wyatt (Bluegrass Special obituary)
claims.source: The HistoryMakers (primary); The Bluegrass Special (secondary), 2012
claims.uncertainty: Low.

entities.name: Warren Avenue Congregational Church
entities.description: 3101 W. Warren Boulevard, East Garfield Park (building now houses New Greater St. John Community Missionary Baptist Church). Served as the West Side headquarters of the SCLC team during the Chicago Freedom Movement.

claims.claim: Warren Avenue Congregational Church was the headquarters of the SCLC team organizing West Side Black Chicagoans to 'end slums'; James Bevel and Bernard LaFayette were the critical leaders.
claims.evidence: Chicago Freedom Movement sites project (Middlebury). Chicago Reporter (2016, excerpt from 'The Chicago Freedom Movement' book): SCLC staff arrived fall 1965 and moved to apartments in East Garfield Park 'closer to the Warren Avenue Congregational Church, which would be their headquarters.'
claims.source: sites.middlebury.edu/chicagofreedommovement/chicago-freedom-movement-sites/; Chicago Reporter, 'The roots of the Chicago Freedom Movement' (2016)
claims.uncertainty: Corroborated by two secondary sources; primary SCLC or Defender confirmation not consulted.

claims.claim: In fall 1965, John McKnight, Midwest Director of the U.S. Commission on Civil Rights, presented on systematic lending discrimination to about 80 SCLC and allied staff in the basement of Warren Avenue Congregational Church.
claims.evidence: Chicago Reporter (2016), excerpt from 'The Chicago Freedom Movement: Martin Luther King Jr. and Civil Rights Activism in the North': presentation 'in the basement of the Warren Avenue Congregational Church on Chicago's West Side' to the Wider Community Staff.
claims.source: Chicago Reporter, 'The Chicago Freedom Movement and the fight for fair lending' (2016)
claims.uncertainty: From a book excerpt; commission records would be primary confirmation.

entities.name: Woodlawn Central
entities.description: Church-led mixed-use development on 8 acres at 63rd and Dorchester in Woodlawn, on land owned by the Apostolic Church of God, developed through ACOG Ventures LLC. Roughly 870 homes, hotel, retail, theater, vertical greenhouse, microgrid; broke ground 2026.

claims.claim: Woodlawn Central is an 8-acre development on land owned by the Apostolic Church of God, planned for roughly 870 homes (affordable, workforce, senior, market-rate, luxury), a 154-160-room hotel, retail, a black-box theater, vertical greenhouse, and microgrid, with a projected 700 permanent jobs; it broke ground in 2026.
claims.evidence: woodlawncentral.com (Transwestern announcement): 8 acres, ~870 homes, 154-room hotel. South Side Builders Association: $895M. PR.com (Feb 2025): ACOG Ventures LLC as self-developer; Phase One hotel, Metra Head House restoration, 140 mixed-income units. J. Byron Brazier op-ed (Black Enterprise, Sept 28, 2026): 'Last month, we broke ground on Woodlawn Central, a $580 million, eight-acre district on land owned by the Apostolic Church of God... roughly 870 homes, a 160-room hotel, retail, a theater, and 700 permanent jobs.'
claims.source: woodlawncentral.com; Black Enterprise, September 28, 2026; PR.com, February 26, 2025
claims.uncertainty: Cost figures vary across sources ($895M in earlier materials vs. $580M in the 2026 op-ed); hotel room count varies (154 vs. 160). Groundbreaking reported by the developer-pastor himself.
